MR. NESBITT  REFERENCE IN DEBATE TO ONE RAYMOND CARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in my remarks last Thursday in connection with the National Housing Act I made reference during the course of my remarks to a civil servant named Raymond Card. My remarks were as follows:
I am informed that Mr. Card came to Canada from England in 1907 and originally set up as an architect. After a brief career in this field he entered the firm of the T. Eaton Company, for which. I am told, he worked as floor manager for some 17 years.
Since that time I have received information from the minister which leads me to the conclusion that, without question, those remarks are not correct. And since I have no desire to be unfair to Mr. Card, or to misrepresent anyone in respect of his qualifications, I should like to have those remarks removed where I state that Mr. Card was an employee of the T. Eaton Company for 17 years. I am quite satisfied he was not, and that he has been an architect ever since he came here.
I might say that I believe the cause for this misinformation was that Mr. Card, who is chief architect for Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, has a brother who was also an architect and who has had business with the T. Eaton Company.

For a copy of all correspondence, telegrams, cablegrams, recorded telephone or other conversations between the government of Canada and any other government authority, person or persons and all documents in the government's possession relating to the trial, death sentence, commuting to a sentence of life imprisonment, the removal from the Canadian prison at Dorchester, New Brunswick, and the further commuting of sentence to imprisonment for fourteen years of Major General Kurt Meyer.

This motion relates to several departments and I have been asked to state the government's position.
Parliament is not the place to try or retry criminal cases of any class and this has always been recognized in the past. Motions for the production of papers relating to trials and remissions of all kinds have not been allowed, as not being in accord with practice or the public interest.
As I stated in the house a few days ago, mixed consultative boards were set up to review sentences of all war criminals still in custody in western Germany. The British high commissioner set up the board to review the cases of all war criminals in custody in the British zone. Meyer and Neitz were among those in custody in the British zone and the Canadian government agreed that they should not be excluded from the review.
The government appointed an outstanding lawyer and a distinguished soldier, Brigadier Sherwood Lett, as observer during the proceedings and to advise the government.
The board recommended that the sentence be reduced to fourteen years. The recommendation was unanimous and it was supported by Brigadier Lett.
So far as is known, every recommendation of every board in every zone has been accepted by the government concerned.
In this case the Canadian government could either reject or accept the recommendation

made by the board and supported by the observer appointed for the purpose. The government of Canada accepted the recommendation. I now table the orders in council giving effect to this decision, dated January 15, 1954, being P.C. 1954/74 and 75. The orders speak for themselves. Of course the government does, as it must, accept full responsibility for them.
For the reasons stated the government is opposing the motion.

Mr. Speaker, I had hoped that this motion might have been accepted by the government because there is no suggestion in this case of a retrial. The circumstances here are not the ordinary circumstances relating to the reconsideration of the punishment due to any convicted member of the armed forces or those who served at one time a former enemy.
Kurt Meyer was found guilty and sentenced to death. Subsequently other steps were taken. We are unaware of the details. Kurt Meyer was transferred from this country under circumstances which left a great deal to the imagination, particularly so far as members of this parliament are concerned. We suddenly found that Kurt Meyer had departed and we did not know whether there had been any previous arrangement. It will be recalled that the suggestion was then made that the spiriting of Kurt Meyer out of Canada at the time was simply preliminary to his subsequent release at an early date. The fears thus expressed have been confirmed by what has taken place.
If there are circumstances which would be disclosed by the material now called for justifying any other decision, then I think we should know of such circumstances. I think it is altogether right and proper, if Kurt Meyer was wrongly dealt with, that his name should be cleared. But a distinction must be drawn between the case of Kurt Meyer and the other cases that were under review.
Those who carry rifles or handle other weapons in the field of battle are entitled to have consideration given to the fact that they are under orders and must obey orders. Officers in command of armies are called upon to interpret the political decisions of governments and there have been cases where that has been given due consideration in dealing with army commanders, even though the conduct of the troops under them may have seemed outrageous and atrocious.
Motions for Papers
But when an officer in command of fighting' troops is found to be guilty of the responsibility, as in this case, extending to the death of young Canadian men in uniform taken-prisoner on the field of battle, that officer" must be held responsible for such an act, or the rules of war will be disregarded at will in the future. At any rate there will be encouragement to follow such a course.
Kurt Meyer either was responsible for the death of young Canadians contrary to the rules of war or he was not. If he was not, then his name should be cleared. If he was, then the procedure that has been followed is not consistent with the best interests of the recognized practices of armies in the field. I submit that this parliament, as the supreme authority in this country, should have the opportunity of examining the exchanges that took place.
I submit that we should know whether there was in fact any prior understanding at the time Kurt Meyer left Canada with the authority and assistance and approval of this government. I submit that we should know whether there was in fact anything in the exchange of correspondence that suggested that a wrong was being righted. I think we should know also, and the parents of young Canadians should know, whether that was the case, or whether a man serving a terrible system was in fact guilty but has been brought almost to the door of freedom for purposes which have not yet been disclosed to this parliament or to the people of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, only a word, the occasion for which arises out of what the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) has said. I think it is evident from what he did say that the purpose for which he is calling for the production of these papers is precisely the purpose for which I suggested that such papers should not be produced. There is no question of the guilt or responsibility of Kurt Meyer involved; that was determined by the court martial. He was found guilty on three out of five counts.
The only question involved subsequent to that was what sentence was proper to be imposed on him. The court martial imposed a sentence of death. That sentence was not valid until it had been confirmed and the death sentence was never confirmed. The confirming officer, acting independently on his own authority, Major General Chris Vokes -a fighting soldier if ever there was one- confirmed the sentence with the sentence of life imprisonment.

Motions for Papers
Kurt Meyer was transferred to Canada to serve his sentence. With the development of events after he had been here some six years it was apparent that he was the only single war criminal convicted of an offence committed in Germany and punished after trial in Germany who was serving his sentence outside of Germany. It was not in order to treat him separately and differently from anyone else that he was transferred back to Germany but in order that his case might be treated precisely the same as every other case of a man sentenced by a similar tribunal and receiving a similar punishment.
On that account he was dealt with just the same way as all other cases were dealt with by the British, French and American authorities in respect of similar cases. Now a tribunal set up by the British authorities in virtue of authority they have and agreed to by us has acted in precisely the same way as tribunals set up by the American and French authorities. In every case, so far as is known to us, the recommendation of the mixed consultative board has been carried out, accepted and acted upon by the government concerned.
Are we in this case going to be the only country to make an exception in respect of this case and treat Kurt Meyer separately and differently from every other war criminal?
May I say just this word.

My hon. friend does not now deal with the question of competence. That was dealt with in the question which he put to me the other day. He now asks me if we would be prepared to send out to the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan officials of our own department who are technically qualified to assist in this matter. I am happy to be able to inform my hon. friend that not only will we be able to do so but that we have already done so. maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Friday, January 22, consideration of the motion of Mr. Winters for the second reading of Bill No. 102, to promote the construction of new houses, the repair and modernization of existing houses, and the improvement of housing and living conditions.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at a rather late hour on Friday night I rose with the intention of adjourning this debate but was encouraged by the minister to make a start. It occurred to me that perhaps he had entertained the hope that I would make a start then and finish and not prolong the agony over the week end. However, on reflection I decided that was a rather cynical point of view, and I was a bit surprised to see that I had already succumbed to the atmosphere of Ottawa. The more charitable interpretation which I have adopted is that the minister really wanted to hear what I had to say and was just impatient on that occasion.
On Friday I was discussing some of the matters pertaining to this bill, and I indicated that I would not deal at any length with part I or attempt to repeat any of the arguments in that connection but would give some attention to parts II and III. The minister mentioned parts II and III in the course of his remarks earlier but did not elaborate upon them and did not point out any greatly needed changes with regard to these particular parts of the bill. I judged from this that the purpose for which parts II and III were designed is being fulfilled, and that nothing further need be done concerning those particular sections of the bill. It is obvious that in any extension of part I, by the filtering down process, which will result in increasing the number of new homes constructed, some benefit will accrue to those people who at present are unable to get rental accommodation or the home ownership accommodation they require. Nevertheless the filtering down process, as we know, works very slowly, and it is measures such as those outlined in parts II and III which are considered necessary, if we are to cope with some of the other problems connected with housing.
I appreciate the fact that difficulty is experienced by some people in understanding the housing situation. On occasion there is an obvious reluctance on the part of certain public bodies to face up to the housing problem, and this is understandable. Time and
1410	HOUSE OF
National Housing Act
again I have had people remark to me, "How can there possibly be a housing shortage when we see all these new developments?" One sees those developments everywhere in Canada. They say, "Why is there still a shortage of houses?"
Of course the reason is twofold. In the first instance, as has been pointed out, family formations have kept pace with the construction of new homes, to a very large extent. Then there is that backlog which has been mentioned by other hon. members-and which I mentioned on Friday night-of anywhere from 100,000 to 500,000 homes, which is not being reduced appreciably by the construction of new homes. Therefore the housing shortage continues, despite the new construction we see all around us.
We are in a transitional period in our civilization. Pioneer days are still a vivid memory, and the adjustment to a more highly organized industrial condition of life is being made slowly. For some people it is difficult, on that account, to appreciate the present problem in the matter of housing. In earlier years the task for many was simply the elementary one of physical labour. I have talked to people who constructed sod houses on the prairies. Anyone who is willing to work could construct that type of accommodation for himself. Similarly a log house could be constructed with little more effort. From that to the frame house was a step depending upon increased income from developed farms.
Governmental assistance and planning was unknown and unexpected. I appreciate the attitude taken by people of the pioneer generation, and by others, who have endured with courage and patience the difficult living conditions they have known. I appreciate the fact that they are not prone to view with enthusiasm any plans that, at first glance, appear merely to afford an easy means of producing luxuries unknown in the earlier period. They realize that life is possible, without all the newfangled gadgets and amenities of modern urban communities.
It is quite true that existence is possible for human beings under primitive conditions. At the same time it is true that bad living conditions exact a heavy toll in disease, in suffering and in reduced expectancy of life. The price paid by earlier generations was the price of a shorter span of life, more suffering from disease and an abnormally high rate of infant mortality.
This leads me to a consideration briefly of the effect of housing on health. As we know, housing is not the only factor that makes for better living or for the improvement of the health of a nation. But it is certainly an 

important factor, and there is plenty of evidence that this is so. In a book published by Edith E. Wood entitled "Housing" she has this to say:
The two nations with the lowest general and infant death rates in the world are Holland and New Zealand. One is old, densely populated, highly urbanized and industrialized; the other is new, sparsely settled and predominantly agricultural. Both have been outstanding in their attention to housing conditions since the turn of the century.
I have not had the pleasure of seeing New Zealand, but a great part of Holland is rather familiar territory. It is a thickly populated country. The houses in the towns and cities are close together, but so far as I could see there are no slums in Holland. There may be, but I could not find them- and I looked for them in the years when I was over there. I looked for them in places that are familiar to many hon. members-Tilburg, Breda, Hertogenbosch, Nijmegen, Apeldoorn. I found no slums, but I did find well-built, substantial homes, even for the poorer classes.
I talked about housing in Holland with a wealthy grain merchant in Tilburg, whose offices we occupied for military purposes. Incidentally he is, or was, an importer of Canadian wheat and an enthusiast for Manitoba No. 1 hard. He informed me, with pride, that not one of his employees was badly housed, and showed me where many of them lived. I visited some of those homes of the working people and found them to be not pretentious dwellings but sturdy brick houses of good appearance, of reasonable size, of obvious comfort and, in typical Dutch fashion, of perfect cleanliness.
In a desire to learn how this had come about, I investigated a little further and gained the information that Holland had embarked upon a housing program as far back as 1901, and had dealt with these matters basically. It was the first attempt on the part of Holland to provide for and to regulate housing in general. Under the legislation then introduced over 10 per cent of the houses in Holland were built by municipalities and public housing societies. Organizations and tenants were permitted to borrow 100 per cent of the cost of their buildings, the buildings to be paid for in 50 years and the land in 75 years.
I have not had the opportunity to investigate further to learn the financial details in this connection, but I simply record these facts as evidence of something I had the pleasure of seeing; and my observations were confirmed by this gentleman in Tilburg, who understood the situation.

Sometimes we are prone to think that Canadians have the highest standard of living in the world. I have never been quite able to understand that phrase, because I do not know how one would go about estimating a standard of living, unless it were merely by a process of counting automobiles, vacuum cleaners, bathtubs, or something like that. If you use the yardstick of housing, Canada has little to boast about and a very great deal to learn. I well recall how surprised Canadian soldiers were when they entered Holland and saw the living conditions of the people in places where the war had not caused destruction.
Again, on the question of housing and its effect on health, I had occasion to delve closely into the book published by Mr. Abrams called "The Future of Housing". He was dealing with the situation in New York city and with the situation in other cities in the United States. The subject that he was discussing was the effect of slums with regard to social evils. May I give a quotation from that book, which is as follows:
That slums breed juvenile delinquency and crime has long been contended. They provide the physical, and encourage the social environment that nourishes growth from truant to juvenile delinquent to felon. The prevalence of a high delinquency rate in slum areas has been established by many authorities and studies ... In one Chicago slum area one out of every four boys between 10 and 17 years appeared in juvenile court in a single year. In Hartford slums, delinquencies were twice as high as in the rest of the city. In Cleveland the rate was three times as high. In Washington, D.C., more than 72 per cent of all juvenile probationers were said to come from overcrowded dwellings . . .
Mr. Abrams investigated the problem of what happens when you rehouse slum dwellers; that is, when the effects of this bill are put into force and slums are cleared away, what happens? Well, the evidence, according to his investigation, was: Fires per 1,000 houses in the new area where the slum had been cleared away and new buildings erected were 2 per 1,000. In an old adjacent slum area similar to the one which had been cleared away, the fires per 1,000 dwellings were 180. Deaths from pneumonia were 2 as contrasted with 14 per 1,000 people, comparing the new cleared area with the old adjacent slum area. Tuberculosis deaths were three times as great in the adjacent slum area. Infant mortality was 2 per 1,000 in the new cleared area as compared to 10 per 1,000 in the old slum area. He then goes on to deal with the excessive costs of public services with regard to those blighted areas and points out in respect to Atlanta, Georgia:
The slum areas of the city contributed 51 per cent of the city's tax revenues from real estate, but 83276-901
National Housing Act
cost the city 53 per cent of its police, fire, health department and other service costs.
It is possible to multiply these examples and draw upon the experience of other countries, but there is no need to go far afield, which I think is unfortunate. We have had surveys in Canada which indicate things somewhat along the same lines. For example, in the city of Winnipeg, and I am quoting from the Winnipeg Tribune of October 24, 1953, we read:
That poor housing is costly to Winnipeg taxpayers and is responsible for higher rates of disease, delinquency and other welfare problems, is shown by a study conducted by the late Mrs. R. F. McWilliams, when she was an alderman in Winnipeg in 1935.
It was found that in two crowded downtown areas scarlet fever and diphtheria cases were 13-6 and 15-7 annually for 1,000 of child population as compared with 7-5 for the rest of the city.
Deaths from tuberculosis were 4-6 and 7-9 annually per 10,000 of population as compared with 2-9 for the rest of the city.
Juvenile court cases were 16-9 and 23-7 per 1,000 pupils as compared with 11-5 for the rest of the city. The excess cost to the city for seven municipal services in these two areas was computed by the deputy city treasurer as being $450,000 annually.
I give the example of Winnipeg merely because it is where I live. I understand and have seen some of the living conditions of the people in that city. I do not think the situation in Winnipeg differs materially from that in other cities across the country.
Those matters of slum clearance and so on are supposed to be dealt with in part III of the bill. Part II of the bill deals with the question of providing rental housing. I have been interested in this for a number of years. It was the first object of interest for me when I returned from overseas in 1946 and entered the Manitoba legislature. At that time I investigated the situation for veterans as far as wartime housing was concerned, and I found that the need for wartime housing exceeded the number available by well over 1,000. The qualifications, you will remember, were: married; overseas service; two or more children. Then, three months ago I inquired again with regard to the wartime housing in Winnipeg and I was informed by those who are responsible that the waiting list at that time was 1,300, a longer waiting list than prevailed in 1946.
I took an interest in emergency shelters in the city of Winnipeg from 1946 on, and became perfectly familiar with emergency shelters that had been set up in the city. There are still emergency shelters in the city of Winnipeg in 1954. According to the report given to the Winnipeg city council not so long ago there are 199 families living in emergency shelters at the present time, and during the course of the year 1953, 932 families applied for emergency accommodation.

National Housing Act Just to indicate the situation I quote two paragraphs from the Winnipeg Tribune of January 14, 1954:
Drafting of a new by-law to enforce higher standards of housing and curb the growth of slums in Winnipeg was recommended today in a report prepared by William Courage, city's emergency housing supervisor.
Mr. Courage reported that living conditions of low-income families with children are more acute now than when the city first set up its housing committee in 1933.
I will show in a minute, Mr. Speaker, why I am drawing attention to these matters of the need of rental housing and the need of slum clearance. But let us consider what the effect of housing is on those who are most seriously concerned. It is interesting to note that in the remarks that were made last week on the question of housing we spoke about- what?-people; about family formation. The number of houses required has a close relation to family formation in the country, and it brings us then of course to a point of interest in that part of our national organization that is most important, and that is the family. We fully agree with and recognize the fact that it is groups of families that form our community and in turn support the superstructure of government on all levels. Unless the family unit is sound all else suffers, and of course the family unit is more concerned with housing than with almost any other problem. Because of faulty housing of families in some areas we are compelled to devote millions of money toward supporting mental institutions, health services, penal institutions and law enforcement services. We lament the growth of delinquency, the increase in divorce, the mounting toll of mental ill-health and the ravages of disease, yet we fail to take adequate measures to counteract the environmental factors that are partly responsible for these social troubles.
That environment contributes to social ills has been proved without shadow of doubt. That adequate housing can assist in preventing the development of these social ills has been clearly demonstrated. If the family unit can be strengthened and maintained under proper circumstances in suitable homes, the children have an opportunity for healthful development.
The nurture and care of children is of prime importance. In their turn they become the working element of the population and provide for and protect the older generation. If the older generation is wise it will ensure that the younger generation is healthy in body and mind. Adequate housing in the interests of the family unit and of the children in particular is sufficient ground for government planning.


We realize that the problem of housing is a difficult one to solve, but to what extent should we urge a solution? I am quite sure that at this point the minister will be prepared to say that the government is perfectly willing to play a part in doing those things which are being advocated to provide rental accommodation and slum clearance and that parts II and III of the act are in the bill for that express purpose. Those parts have been operative for some time. I ask the minister: Why is it, if those parts are satisfactory, that we still have these problems of the lack of rental accommodation and the development of slums?
I was discouraged to read that William Courage had reported to the city of Winnipeg that some action must be taken to curb the growth of slums. I had hoped that at this stage we would have come sufficiently to grips with the problem that there would be no further growth of slum conditions.
I suggest to the minister that when he was rewriting the parts of this bill he should have given more attention to parts II and III. I think we should have a picture given to us of how these parts have operated in the past and what effect they are producing. We should have indicated to us why they are not measuring up to our expectations.
The burden is not solely with the dominion government as the provinces and municipalities have to play their part. I wonder if the problem does not arise because of the situation in which the municipalities have been placed. When the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) was speaking the other day he quoted from a statement by the minister in which it was indicated that one of the great bottlenecks, perhaps the largest in connection with the problem of housing, was the provision of serviced land, that it was the inability of municipalities to provide serviced land that helped to create the bottleneck. Then the hon. member for Eglinton made a comment which I think deserves repetition and I quote from page 1321 of Hansard of January 21:
The municipalities of this country, sir, are functioning today with virtually the same tax base that was given to them at the time of confederation. And, with the rapidly soaring costs of providing municipal services, demanded by all residents, it has become beyond the power of municipalities to meet the responsibilities they are now expected to discharge under existing legislation.
My observation of municipal government is that it does set a very good example in this country of efficiency and economy, but it has been pointed out time and time again in this house that in recent years the municipalities have been curbed because of their

lack of financial strength. Should not the minister give some attention to this? If the municipalities are unable to meet the fairly generous offers contained in parts II and III of the bill, then a review of the situation should be considered. Let us make it possible for the municipalities to deal with these problems which are affecting them adversely in so many ways.
I would conclude with one remark. In so far as rental accommodation is not provided to meet the needs of our people, in so far as slum clearance is not proceeded with vigorously and with dispatch, to that extent the present bill falls far short of what is desired.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I intend to speak but briefly on this bill. While I was sitting here thinking of what I might say when I got up, and making a note or two upon which I might base what I had to say, I had interjected into my thinking a statement by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) a few minutes ago when he said that he did not intend to initiate any move at the moment to combat unemployment for the reasons which he stated. I have no doubt that he was sincere in stating those reasons. One reason given was that it was merely a temporary condition. I do not think that this new bill in regard to housing will have much effect upon the unemployment situation. I sincerely do not think that it will result in the building of many more houses than would have been built under the original act.
I wish the government would show some bold imagination in this connection. In spite of the fact that you might have called me to order on my first sentence, I do submit that there is some connection between the two subjects of housing and unemployment. If we had a bold imaginative program for subsidized rental housing, if we had a government scheme instead of the government retreating from housing; if they would get into it wholeheartedly; if they would set some of these unemployed people to work; if they would give them employment with the hope that they would earn sufficient money to get into a house on any terms; then I think the government would be doing something worth while.
I must say that I think that up to now the government has been bankrupt of ideas in regard to both unemployment and housing. That may be rough criticism, but that is what I think. As long as this government is in power I do not think that we will have our people properly and sufficiently housed. I am a great believer in the ownership of homes. The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) has referred to the necessity
National Housing Act
of having a good environment for children. Needless to say I am entirely in agreement with that statement.
I have shown some interest in this house in young people, in their education and in their health. I feel quite convinced that those two things affect the rising generation. It is the same with a home. Let every man sit under his own fig tree. I hope he can. But if he cannot have a fig tree of his own, I hope he can at least find a fig tree. In other words,, if it is impossible for him to own a house then it should be possible for him to rent one according to what the economic condition of the country allows him to pay.
In my own city of Saskatoon we are getting along reasonably well with housing. Some hon. members may know that we have various housing schemes under the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation which are going along all right, except that some of my friends who are in the contracting business claim they are not getting enough of them. But they can fight that out with the minister.
We are being helped too in the matter of rental housing by the fact that one or two outside firms are coming into the city and will begin extensive building this spring. That will help to ease the situation but there are still many people, in spite of the fact that, as I believe, living conditions there are as good as any in Canada, who are still living in quarters where three and four families are using the same bathroom. These are the so-called suites. I need not tell hon. members that some of these suites that are available to rent usually comprise a room with something that I think some would call a kitchenette, but which you and I would call a clothes closet, with one electric burner or unit on which perhaps you could fry an egg if you were lucky.
There is one matter I wish to draw to the attention of the minister which arises out of various complaints I have received. Many people have approached me, young men, who have gone into Central Mortgage housing schemes and they have discovered after being in the houses weeks or perhaps a few months, after putting money into them, that there were faults in the houses such as cracks in the basement, and badly fitting doors or something wrong with the construction. They try to do something about it and are told that once the contractor has been paid out there is really nothing that can be done about it. "You should have spoken earlier", is the answer they get.
I would suggest it takes time and a certain amount of living in a house to discover whether it meets your expectations or not.

As regards the bill itself, on the face of it it looks to me like a plan which, whatever its intention may be, will result in putting a larger number of people into a larger amount of debt over a longer period of time. This bill does not set out a definite rate of interest. We have been given to understand that the rate of interest will probably be 5f per cent. Mr. Speaker, I should like to take part in this debate on the new housing legislation which was recently introduced by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters). I do so for several reasons. This legislation is an attempt to make provision for what is commonly admitted to be perhaps the most glaring and serious need of the people of this country. This problem has contributed, perhaps more than any other, to many of the negative repercussions of this cocktail age in which you and I live. For this reason I believe this measure is one of the most important ones which have come before this session of parliament and certainly deserves the widest of discussion. Anything I may say is said in good faith and is certainly not meant to detract in any way from the efforts of the minister, incomplete as they are, to alleviate the situation.
I have the honour of representing in this house a constituency in a city which, on a per capita basis, has one of the highest figures for construction of any city on the North American continent. When over 50 per cent of the construction permits issued in that city were for the purpose of building homes, it stands to reason that this matter is one
1416	HOUSE OF
National Housing Act
which is of great concern to me because it affects the well-being of the people I represent. In order that it may serve as a background to anything further which I may have to say on this matter, I should like to read what I consider to be an extremely interesting report that appeared in the Financial Times of January 22, 1954. It is entitled, "Growth of Edmonton Shows Top Building Rate Per Capita" and reads in part as follows:
At the beginning of its fiftieth anniversary year, Edmonton stands in a class by itself among the larger cities of North America . . .
Computed on a per capita basis, construction in Edmonton last year was much greater than in any other city on the continent . . .
Though many millions of dollars are being spent on industrial construction in Edmonton, it is encouraging to the city's increasing population that nearly half of the total building permits issued during 1953 were for housing construction.
All signs point to another record year in this direction in 1954. This is essential if the city is to keep pace with its rapid growth.
Edmonton is now estimated to have a population of 193,000. At its present rate of growth of 8 per cent, this figure will be very close to 200,000 by early summer. Moreover, if this rate of gain is maintained, the city will reach 300,000 by 1959.
This matter of housing legislation, Mr. Speaker, involves more than just bricks and the materials going into the construction of a home. It involves shelter in the full meaning of that word. We know that homes are crucial for the well-being of any nation. Homes means greater population. Homes mean a happy people; and a happy people means an unconquerable nation. The unhappiness, delinquency and crime which this housing situation have brought about in our country cannot be measured. In the press and in past parliaments there has been a great deal of discussion of the necessity for encouraging cultural growth in our great country. I maintain there is a definite community of interest between family life-the home-and further cultural growth. It seems strange to me, as a new member, that at a time such as this we should be spending millions for guns, bombs and tanks and yet permit the deplorable situation in housing to exist. I should like to say that I have no quarrel with defence. In the face of what we see in the world today we have no alternative. But it does seem strange that we are able to solve the problem of defence and are not able to apply the same maximum effort in matters which have to do with internal conditions. While we have been vigilant on the military front, we have at the same time [DOT]been absolutely negligent with respect to something that is just as important, the internal front.
r.Mr. Holowach.]

The history of nations in recent years shows us quite vividly that countries with tremendous defence set-ups have fallen to negative moral forces because their governments had failed to pay any attention to the crippling and demoralizing economic and social injustices in their lands. I think this should be remembered when this legislation goes before the banking and commerce committee. I think that the key to an understanding of the problem facing us can be found by comparison. During the depression years we needed homes badly. We had the skills and materials and unemployed men who were ready to do the job, but one thing was basically lacking. The people did not have the money. Today we have an equivalent situation. We need homes desperately. We have the skills and materials and better techniques. We have unemployment, and yet people today lack the basic purchasing power necessary to acquire the things that they need.
In order to verify what I have just stated I should like to quote a most revealing bit of information from the Ottawa Journal of January 19. The article is headed, "Credit Buying Hit New High September" and reads in part as follows:
Another boost in instalment-plan buying pushed Canada's consumer credit bill to a new high of $1,772 million on September 30 . . . The major share of the increase was in finance company dealings. Their outstanding credit rose to $544 million on September 30 from $516 million on June 30. Instalment credit by retail dealers increased by $5 million to $248 million from $243 million.
It seems to me that is a very good indication that, so far as the people are concerned, what is most lacking today is the purchasing power to take advantage of the scheme that the government has presented. For the past few days we have listened to a dissection of this legislation, and what does the autopsy show? I think it would be quite right to say that it is the same old body dressed up in the same old suit. The only difference is that there are a few patches which I do not think will give any amount of comfort or aid in securing the basic needs of the people today with respect to housing legislation.
It is admitted that in the bill there are several new features which are commendable. The banks will be induced and encouraged to enter the mortgage business, and payments will be spread over a longer period. But there seems to be no provision or inducement to reduce interest rates and construction costs. There is no provision to protect the equity of a defaulter, and I do not quite understand how anyone earning less than $3,000 can take advantage of the plan now presented. I believe that the Canada Year Book indicates

that for the year 1950 three-quarters of a million people in Canada fell within that income tax bracket. I think we should bear this in mind when we are considering this legislation.
During the past few days most of the criticism of the bill has come from members of the opposition, and I should like to hear some of the government members express their views with respect to it. As grown-up men and women we should realize that patting one another on the back and following party lines in matters of this kind will not bring about betterment. I know of no progressive legislation that has not been brought about by a united protest. This matter is of the greatest importance to the Canadian people. As a matter of fact, I think it has a most serious implication. It places parliament on trial. Our ability to solve the housing problem in Canada will strengthen the faith of the people of Canada in the ability of parliament to get down to business and tackle a serious problem. It will strengthen the faith of our people in democracy and set a shining example for those who condemn it. I think our failure to do so will strengthen the hand and the voice of those who say that democracy cannot bring about improvement and must be replaced by some form of "ism."
Various suggestions have been made. In the first place, I believe that the interest rate is far too high. What is wrong with lowering the interest rate to 3J per cent for those who earn less than $3,000 a year? At the present time banking institutions pay 2 per cent on depositors' money. It seems to me that what is sauce for the goose should certainly be sauce for the gander. Nobody has any criticism of the important part our banking institutions play. They have a most important function to perform, but I think that they, as well as every other agency, should realize that this is the zero hour from the point of view of making sacrifices and that their sacrifice so far as profits are concerned should be just as great as the sacrifice of people who now have to suffer the discomforts of not having a home.
As a new member I have watched and studied with a great deal of interest the activities of the various cabinet ministers and have listened to them with great interest when they have been in action on the floor of the house. From where I sit the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters) strikes me as being a very capable, sincere young man. I do not know too much about his political past, but I would say that, having been in politics but a short while, he certainly has not become hardened or indifferent to the
National Housing Act
needs of the people. I submit to him that when this matter comes before the banking and commerce committee he should use his good offices to see that the interest rate is lowered, that some inducement in the form of lower income tax is offered to people who have to carry the extra burden of paying for a home, and that some attempt is made to lower the terrifically high construction costs.
I think this could be done by the declaration of a definite building target for 1954. It would certainly contribute to stabilizing employment. It would enable the various construction firms to make definite plans for the future and would eliminate the valley of ups and downs so far as employment is concerned. Here is an opportunity for the minister to really take a bold and broad step forward in meeting the needs of the people. It is an opportunity for him to be marked in Canadian history as one who has done much.
One thing further I would say and it has not been said before in the debate. As a matter of fact certain inferences have been drawn which are not true so far as the Canadian people are concerned. One of their most prominent characteristics, it seems to me, is a spirit of independence and a willingness to assume responsibility. They do not seek any form of handout, because they know there is no such animal. In any event they would have to pay the price for it. But they do insist that we, as their representatives, understand the financial situation confronting them and that we bear in mind the fact that this legislation, as in respect of all other legislation dealing with the well-being of the people, must be geared to assist those who are not now in a position to afford homes, rather than make it easier for those who are. Unless this is done, then it would seem that the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) was right on Friday night when he said that this legislation is only another step to perpetuate this government's moth-eaten financial policy.
In conclusion, I would like to see justice and fair play for the Canadian people, and an effort to make available, particularly to the low income groups, the homes which are so sorely needed. While this legislation in its present form may be expedient from a political standpoint, it is certainly not right in principle and does not answer the demand the people are making upon parliament today.

Mr. Speaker, speaking in this debate on January 22, the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary (Mr. Jones) said:
-these people are not anxious to live in these shacks, they cannot meet the requirements of this

National Housing Act
bill or any government legislation that has ever existed so far as the securing of a home is concerned.
In my opinion it is not any defect in the housing act that causes people to live in shacks, but rather the excessive cost of housing in our time. The National Housing Act cannot be blamed for the fact that housing is as costly as it is today.
Speaking in the debate on January 21 the minister said:
The period of amortization for home ownership loans, including co-operative housing associations and rural housing, will be 25 years as a minimum and 30 years as a maximum. However, the borrower will be able to arrange for a shorter term if he so indicates in writing.
Earlier he stated:
It will be recalled that at the present time the maximum loan is $10,000 for home ownership. In setting the limit of loan one consideration will be that the present cost of residential construction is about 25 per cent higher than it was when the $10,000 was set.
If my memory serves me correctly it was in 1950 or 1951 that the $10,000 figure was set, so this means an increase of 25 per cent in the cost of housing since that time. When we speak of the high cost of living at this particular period and compare it with the pre-war period we say that our dollar is worth 56 cents. Others say that it is worth less than 50 cents. For the purposes of my argument, however, I shall say that it has 50 per cent of its 1939 value, or that it is worth 50 cents.
An automobile that cost about $1,300 in 1939 will now sell for about $2,600, or an increase of 100 per cent. I have actual figures for the cost of houses in 1939, but for purposes of simplicity I shall use round figures and say that a house which then cost $2,500 would cost between $8,000 and $9,000 today. This is almost four times the cost of the pre-war article.
When purchasing an automobile today everyone seeks a certain amount of individuality, but in the purchase of homes people are going even farther. It would seem that every home must have its own individual design to suit the taste of the purchaser. We will either have to forget this demand for individuality or be content to pay these excessive costs. Whether one buys a low priced automobile or one in the $5,000 or $6,000 class he will find that, essentially, they are the same in outline, and that the differences are chiefly in the matter of colour. One's individuality is given scope in his choice of paint, or in the chrome used. I believe that in a home one's individuality could be shown in the upkeep of the home

or in the condition in which the yard is kept. It is not necessary that every house be different in appearance.
If there is a continuation of this demand for individuality it will be impossible to use the prefabricated article, which is so desirable at the moment. Great quantities of lumber are available in British Columbia which would be quite suitable for prefabricated homes. Insulation when applied to frame houses makes them acceptable, and I think it is within reason to believe that prefabricated homes can be built at costs lower than those quoted today.
I believe it is essential that the government take the lead in an effort to find ways and means to have the builders and the unions sit down with government officials to work out some policy whereby homes may be provided at prices within the ability of average wage earners to pay. If necessary a royal commission could be set up to go into this serious matter and ascertain why the cost of housing has got so far out of line when compared with the cost of other commodities.
If a man earning $2,500 to $3,000 attempts to purchase a home with a capital cost of $10,000 to $12,000, and undertakes to pay the normal interest charges for adequate financing, he will be in slavery for well over a third of his natural working life. That is a very unhealthy situation, and I believe something should be done. It is not only necessary to make provision for more capital, because capital is merely a measure of the goods themselves, and more -capital does not mean that we are going to have more houses until the prices of houses are brought more nearly in line with the salary of the average wage earner today.
While we are doing an excellent job, I am sure there is not going to be any appreciable difference in the number of houses that will be built within the next year. I predict that owing to the greater amount, as we hope, of capital becoming available there will be throughout the year a greater increase in the cost of these houses.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it requires a certain amount of hardihood to enter a debate on the third day, even a debate of the importance of the one we are engaged in now. I think I should not have that hardihood except that I believe the bill before us invites us to confer powers so broad, so far-reaching, and above all so permanent on this government institution that I still cling to the hope that it may be possible to achieve the end desired, and

which of course is eminently desired by us all, without the necessity of having recourse to the tremendous powers which are given. These powers incidentally seem to relegate private enterprise, which is nailed to the mast, so to speak, of our party, and which I think the government would say is also nailed to their mast, to the position of a mere machine which is going to be used by this government organization. There will be precious little freedom left in the housebuilding and the house-investing industry, so far as I can see, if this bill passes unchanged.
Let me make one thing perfectly clear. There is nobody who can possibly be anything but favourable to the declared purpose of the bill, which I will read:
An act to promote the construction of new houses, the repair and modernization of existing houses, and the improvement of housing and living conditions.
Everybody has to approve of that, but of course it is possible to do the right thing in the wrong way, and I thoroughly believe that in some respects this is the wrong way.
I am not going to get involved in many details which have been dealt with admirably by my colleagues in this house, but there are certain general points that I do wish to discuss. The first thing that strikes me about this is that the government gave themselves every chance, it seems to me, to go the wrong way; because so far as any of us know this plan was worked out in splendid isolation in one of the government's ivory towers. Those people who have so fully and effectively co-operated with the government in making house loans for a good many years-I refer to the lending institutions- were not consulted. The institutions who it is hoped are going to take up the load, or a good part of the load from now on, namely the banks, were not consulted.
Now, as I reflect, I wonder whether perhaps the only people who may have been consulted at all are people outside the country. This plan, I take it, is modelled very largely on the position in the United States, and it may be, though we do not know, that there was consultation there. There is no point in my asking at length why there has been no discussion. There are of course governments who do not believe in discussion. We think of the totalitarian governments, and we know that to expect them to discuss is just silly. They do not discuss things, but it is surprising that it should happen here.
1 have asked myself why it has happened. I have reminded myself that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), when
National Housing Act
he has a public enterprise under his control, thinks of it as very much his own enterprise. Whether the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters), who is still early in his official career, has already caught up with the Minister of Trade and Commerce and -has come to regard these institutions as his own, I do not know. He does not convey that impression, of course. He tries to make us feel that our opinion is of value, that we are being consulted, but there are the facts, such as they are.
Of course we all do admit that there are cases where obviously governments cannot consult. We do not expect the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) to come and consult with us at the last moment as to just what changes he is going to make in the income tax, and incidentally I doubt whether the minister is going to consult very much with this house in future in any event, because of a certain unfortunate experience that he did have.

Oh, yes, I am sure they were, but as I say it was a delay-action consultation.
Now, there is another thing that handicaps us a bit at the moment, and I hope it will be set right before we get too far into the

National Housing Act committee. It is that this bill has another unfortunate-what shall I say-feature that so many bills have. That is, just as you are getting to something very important you find, "The governor in council will make regulations to cover this." The regulations of course are not public. On the other hand they are not entirely secret, either. They sort of leak out from time to time. But I do hope that when we come to the committee we shall have the regulations and we shall not have to approve the bill without the regulations before us. In other words, we shall not have to go to the play with Hamlet left out.
Now a word as to the public reception of the bill. I would never deny that the government publicity is always good. I think there was the usual built-up enthusiasm which we are so accustomed to seeing, at the very first announcement; but as people had time to look at it a rather different attitude sprang up. People felt that they would be wise to "stop, look and listen." I refer very briefly to some words from the Regina Leader-Post of December 22, which bear that out. They are as follows:
Glib references to a ten per cent down payment are likely to conjure up images that anyone who wants and needs a house will be able to buy one by going through somewhat the same procedure as plunking down $25 on a $250 refrigerator which in a matter of hours is ensconced in the family kitchen.
Reginans who have been dreaming of the yet unattainable cosy home might as well face the fact now, as they inevitably may have to do later, that no such alluring prospect may be in store for them.
Just a word as to the history of this thing. As it has been covered before I shall not do more than mention it. I think it was in 1935 that the first legislation was passed, just before the change of government. That was followed by legislation put through by Mr. Dunning, and under the National Housing Act there has been a successful partnership which worked pretty well on the basis of an 80 per cent loan, 25 per cent participation by the government and 75 per cent by the lending institutions.
The figures for last year are very important. The results achieved in 11 months of 1953 showed $239 million as the amount put out in joint loans, and I believe $51 million by Central Mortgage alone. On the basis of $239 million for 11 months I take it to work out to something in the nature of $260 million for the year.
As I said a moment ago, this was changed without any warning. Notice was given by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) on October 1 that this was going to be changed. It was felt that enough money was not
[Mr. Macdonnell.l

likely to be forthcoming this year; therefore the change with which we are familiar was proposed.
As I have said, there are many points of criticism which have been carefully made and which I have no desire to repeat. But there is one thing that I do desire to repeat, because I believe it is so important. I think it is unfortunate, and it seems to me that it perhaps is a necessary characteristic of bureaucracy, but it just shows how much one loses when one is forced away from ordinary human dealings between man and man and gets into the hands of a bureaucracy. I am not saying that with disrespect, as I have great respect for the president of Central Mortgage, I am only saying that there are certain things a huge bureaucracy cannot do, and I refer to them in this manner.
We are bringing in borrowers, purchasers of houses who are going to pay for them on the instalment plan. As the president of the Royal Bank of Canada said the other day, we have become a pretty high-cost economy. I will not dwell on the fact, which I have mentioned before and may mention again, that that is not at all unrelated to the easy money policies which were followed by this government and which were nice and easy for those who get the easy money but which become more and more difficult for those who do not share in the easy money.
That helped to raise prices. We all know that the rise in building costs was very much above the average. So these prices, to which I shall not refer at length, have gone up. I had hoped incidentally that suggestions which have been made as to the possibility of much lower prices even though not on exactly the same standards of construction, might be seriously considered by the minister.
I come back now to these borrowers. If they are just human beings like the rest of us the chances are they will have some other instalment payments to make beyond the payments on their houses. They may very well be making payments on a car, on a radio or what you will. What I am coming to is this. In all probability a good many of these people will be under strain in making their payments.
When an individual borrows from a good lender-I shall try to explain in a moment what I think a good lender is, and on this subject I have some experience-he knows that the last thing in the world that lender wants to do is to take his property. That is not from any high or altruistic motives, though I would say that there have been far more good relations between borrower and

lender throughout this country than sometimes people like to admit. However, I just put it on the ground of good business. No lender wants to take over the property of a private borrower who has lived up to the character which the lender believed he had and who is doing his best to work out his loan.
Let us see what is going to happen here, because here is where bureaucracy comes in. It has been pointed out, and I do not intend to refer to it at great length, that there is an escape clause; but the genius of this act is that the lender, who is being guaranteed, bias to be right on the job and not leave any opening so it can be said that he was slack in pressing for his money. If that is what we are led to understand from, shall I say, unofficial reports of the regulations, he may easily get into difficulty. So I just want to make this point-

speechtext:
What I understand to be in them-of course the sections of the act are pretty stiff too-is that the lender, unless there are unusual circumstances, will have to give practically no leeway. He will have to go ahead and enforce his security. I point out that this is one of the difficulties with a
National Housing Act
huge bureaucracy. You are faced with the dilemma of it either being ridden with politics, which none of us want but which could happen, or it has to act in a rigid and unyielding manner. I do not think we shall be able to blame them. I think Central Mortgage will have duties laid on them which will compel them to do this. Therefore I am making the point that to me one of the most unfortunate things about this is that the lender will not be able to put off the foreclosure even for years if he believes the borrower is doing his best and that he is not only honourable but capable.
I have said that there was a fruitful partnership between the lending institutions and Central Mortgage, but that the form in which it worked it is being done away with and that Central Mortgage is proposing to withdraw from the 25-75 relationship. We are all aware of how that is to be taken care of. Central Mortgage will still be able to make loans itself, but as regards the others they will be dealt with by insurance policies. The money is supposed to come from private institutions and is to be guaranteed. How much money will be needed is anyone's guess. I gave the figures a moment ago to indicate that last year the total amounts put out jointly by the lending institutions and Central Mortgage were somewhere in the neighbourhood of $260 million. Central Mortgage will not now supply its 25 per cent of that, and it is expected that the lending institutions will not be able to supply quite so much. I suppose a fair guess might be that there may be something like $100 million or more needed. I put that forward purely as a rough guess.
A word about the availability of funds. The banks of course have declared their readiness to co-operate and on this point there has been some interesting comments, some by the Bank of Canada and some at the annual meetings of the banks themselves, indicating their approach. Bank loans are very high, and they have increased by some $600 million their ordinary commercial loans in the last year. In a manner of speaking it has been customary to say that the banks are "fully loaned" but I think it is a dangerous phrase to use, because after all, in spite of the fact that a year ago the banks were pretty well loaned up, last year loans were increased by the very substantial amount I have mentioned. The question then arises as to the banks' reserves and I will refer to that in a moment.
On the question of liquidity-a word I think has almost fallen out of use in our vocabulary, at least as far as money matters are concerned, and which I think we should

National Housing Act
recognize as of great importance-it is interesting to point out that within the last few days there appeared in the press a reference to the reserves of the chartered banks. That reference contains the following, and I am quoting from the Montreal Gazette of January 22, 1954:
A broad change in the mechanics of credit control by the Bank of Canada is under study by the government and may be translated into legislation.
A proposal, which follows upon the decision of the government to permit banks to lend on new residential construction is that the cash ratio chartered banks must maintain against deposit liabilities shall be variable and shall be altered by the Bank of Canada according to the position of the economy.
The statutory position now, substantially unchanged since the Bank of Canada came into existence in 1935, is that the chartered banks must maintain with the Bank of Canada not less than 5 per cent of their deposit liabilities. In practice this has been generally conceded to be unrealistic and the ratio has been kept in the neighbourhood of 10 per cent.
What is likely to happen, if present plans mature, is that the Bank of Canada will from time to time set a minimum ratio that may vary from 8 per cent to 12 per cent according to circumstances.
As you will observe, Mr. Speaker, that is really following what has actually been the practice. In other words the banks have not been content to maintain the legal minimum of 5 per cent, but practice has fixed it at about 10 per cent. Indeed, 10 per cent is used as almost a legislative figure. That 10 per cent is the amount by which the banks may increase credit facilities as they increase cash. In other words, they apply the 10 per cent figure and not the 5 per cent figure.
I want to draw attention to a recent comment by a banker, because on the one hand I think we can take it for granted that the banks will co-operate to the best of their ability, and on the other hand I think we should bear in mind that it is not just a question of looking at the amount of deposits in a bank and saying there is a lot of money there and they can lend hundreds and hundreds of millions of dollars. I am reading from a report in the Toronto Globe and Mail dated January 21, 1954, part of which is the Globe's own comment and part of which contains the words of Mr. Vanstone, president of the Bank of Toronto. The first part is the Globe's summary of what Mr. Vanstone said, and when I come to Mr. Vanstone's own words I will indicate them:
Mr. Vanstone agrees that it is right and proper for the maximum number of Canadians to live in their own houses. To do that construction and financing costs must remain within their capacity to pay. If public funds are to be considered essential to add to private funds to aid in financing house buying, dwelling units should be of the most economical type of construction consistent with durability, sanitation and propriety. Hitherto life insurance, mortgage and trust companies and 

private investors have been the traditional sources of mortgage funds. House mortgages were made a lawful investment for trust funds and practically everything had been done to put them in a preferred position to attract funds for which immediate liquidity was not necessary.
The need for liquidity had dominated banking since before confederation.
Now I come to Mr. Vanstone's own words:
Depositors in Canada's chartered banks consider that they are placing their money on demand.
It is true that savings accounts have legally a 10 day delay, but no bank would ever dream of invoking that delay. Mr. Vanstone continues:
Only by in turn placing their depositors' money in constantly maturing, short-term loans to business or in sound marketable public securities, can the banks be certain of not disappointing them.
That is the depositors.
Inasmuch as there is a hard core of savings deposits which in effect form personal reserves likely to be called for only in personal emergency, it may be that the banks can without undue risk depart from total short-term liquidity to place some small portion of these funds in well-secured mortgages and thereby be in a position to perform a public service by filling such gaps in the market for housing capital as existing financial agencies may not quite cover. Obviously the extent to which this can be done will depend on the degree of liquidity that the government is willing to make available if and when necessary, and it is only to a moderate extent that it would be prudent to tie up the funds of Canadian depositors in long-term fixed investments.
The banks must keep themselves in a position to take care of demands from depositors and fully look after the requirements of trade and commerce.
Now, in the light of this let us look at the statement made by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) which started this discussion last October. I read briefly from his speech as reported in the Ottawa Journal of October 1, 1953:
The government does not believe that it would be sound under present conditions to fill the gap-
That is the gap caused by the expected inability of the lending institutions to provide all the money.
-by direct government lending.
If that were done the government would become the direct mortgagee or landlord of a large number of Canadian families.
The Prime Minister continued:
The government feels that the proper solution is to enlarge and broaden the supply of mortgage money by making mortgages more attractive and a more liquid form of investment than they have been up to now.
I wish to comment briefly on the Prime Minister's statement. He does not think it would be sound under present conditions "to fill the gap by direct government lending". That does not seem to me to be a very realistic statement because the government is actually the person responsible, though in

the background. When you consider that the government is behind Central Mortgage, and that Central Mortgage is guaranteeing the loans, it seems to me that it is a distinction very largely without a difference.
The Prime Minister then went on to say that it is not the government's wish to "become the direct mortgagee or landlord of a large number of Canadian families". He considers it very undesirable, and so do I. Nevertheless, if in fact Central Mortgage is going to assume that position I do not see that it is any great comfort to us. You will observe, Mr. Speaker, that the Prime Minister uses the word "landlord" as well as "mortgagee", by which I assume he means that by reason of defaults there is a possibility of properties having to be taken over.
I want to deal now briefly with the question of liquidity. Liquidity, as I said a moment ago, has nothing to do with the temperance act. It has to do with the availability of money on depositors' demand. Commenting on the Prime Minister's statement about mortgages being made more liquid, Saturday's edition of the Montreal Gazette has the following to say:
Graham Towers, governor of the Bank of Canada, said the bank probably will be allowed loans up to 100 per cent of the value of mortgages, but in practice this is not done. Their borrowing from the central bank was only for moderately small amounts and for short periods.
The period is indeed short enough, because under the Bank of Canada Act, section 18, loans are supposed to be for six months. That would not open the door very wide though, as a matter of fact, I suppose in actual practice if the banks went to the Bank of Canada for additional money they would probably use as their first line of defence not their mortgages but government of Canada bonds and other securities which they have.
In passing I want to point out that I think this whole plan is based largely on the practice followed by United States banks. I further point out that it was done there in the midst of the depression. It was a depression measure. It seems to me to be unfortunate if we have to follow somewhat slavishly, in a time which is certainly not a time of depression, what the Americans did at a time of depression.
I want to digress just for a moment further on the question of the amount available. That is a matter that is going to be undoubtedly in the discretion of the Bank of Canada. I think that is clear. It will depend upon how much further cash they are prepared to provide the chartered banks so the chartered banks may turn around and make these mortgage loans. As I said, it is interesting that
National Housing Act
at the very moment this matter comes up, there is a suggestion of increasing the percentage of reserves required.
May I spend just a moment on the question of liquidity. The banks take deposits, and of course their only means of earning is to make those deposits work. They lend those deposits out, and they have to judge the likely requirements or the likely demands of depositors. Of course it is fatal to any bank if they are ever caught without enough money to satisfy the demands of depositors. It is important to distinguish between security and liquidity. In the crash in the United States in 1932 there were banks which had plenty of assets with which to pay all the depositors but which could not be realized on demand. It is no good to tell a depositor who wants his money today that you have a loan coming in next week, next month or next year. If you cannot pay upon demand, your doors close. There were many banks at that time whose doors closed, though eventually they were able to pay off in full.
It will be obvious to hon. members that, as you might say, the three lines of defence a bank has are, first, its cash reserves; second, government bonds and other quickly realizable securities; and third, commercial paper and that kind of thing which represents money lent on short terms and which is being repaid day by day.
At the outset I complained about this bill which erects this huge bureaucracy and which leaves so little to be done by private enterprise. I want to quote briefly from words used by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) which I think are worth repeating. Speaking of the powers of the bill, as reported at page 1333 of Hansard he said:
The powers are so vast that those of us who do not trust power in the hands of the government will not feel that powers of this nature, powers which are so wide, so sweeping and so inclusive are needed.
There is one point that I should like to make here and it is this. We have had many cases where there have been sweeping emergency powers, with regard to foreign exchange control and other matters, where we have differed-where there have been different feelings-as to how long they should last. But I think I am correct in saying that in those cases there was always or almost always agreement among us that the power in question was for an emergency, for a special purpose, and that the time would come when it would disappear. With respect to this bill it seems to me that the situation is exactly the opposite. There is no reason to believe that it will disappear. Quite the contrary; I think it

National Housing Act
will become more and more deeply embedded, and that it will exercise more and more authority in this part of the lending industry which, after all, is a large area of our whole economy. As time goes on, I think the approved lending institutions may find that it is almost a waste of time for them to keep up the organizations which they have at the present time and which have been so active, as the minister knows, in arriving at sound valuations.
The best information I can get in connection with the similar practice in the United States is that the approved lending institutions there still take the responsibility of making the valuations, though they may be checked up-as indeed our own valuations have been checked up-to some extent by the public body.
But as the situation stands, as the minister well knows, every approved lending institution must await the nod from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation before it acts. If it is a building loan, there must be a detailed, meticulous report and approval by Central Mortgage; and let anyone beware of disregarding the slightest wish of Central Mortgage because, as we all know, guarantees are tricky things and his guarantee might be called in question.
As I said a moment ago, the only place where initiative is still left to the lender is in the dirty job of foreclosing loans. He is not only left with that job but he is forced to do it, even though it may be entirely against his own better judgment.
I said at the outset that nobody can read the legend on the outside of this bill without approving it, but I wish to say that I still hope that in committee it may not be found necessary to go nearly the length of these wide, inclusive, meticulous and permanent powers. I want to say here that to me, despite everything that may have been intended, this is a great step forward into state socialism. What we are having here is the part played by private enterprise-which up to the present has been great-really being played down. Private enterprise is going to be just the agent of this new institution.
I wish to make a few comments on that matter, because to me it is striking at the very root of what I believe to be the motive power of our economic life. Most of us in this chamber differ from the socialists on that matter. I would think the socialists would find this legislation extremely palatable. If they do not, I shall have lost confidence in their judgment. After all, it is going along the line they themselves so often advocate.

I want to draw attention to the fact that in England there has obviously been a revulsion of feeling. I drew this to the attention of the house before. At the Margate convention again and again measures to further public enterprise were voted down. I refer to the trade union congress at Margate.
I often find that the socialists seem to regard wealth as if it were a fixed amount and it were only a question of dividing it up.
I have been greatly interested to find the extent to which leading socialists apparently have turned their faces in a different direction. I have here a book the title of which will not immediately commend itself to hon. gentlemen opposite because it is called "The Conservative Mind". But I should like to make two comments with regard to that book. One is that the "c" is a small "c", and the other is that it was strongly recommended to me by one of the best-known gentlemen who sit opposite in this house. In it there are two or three short quotations I should like to read because they indicate such a great change of attitude. One is this:
Finding that the majority of men seem to lack motive for performing their duties in society, now that the ordinary rewards for ordinary integrity have been abolished or diminished, the socialists are dismayed; they begin to wonder whether their theory of human nature can be at fault. Professor G. D. H. Cole says that "socialism is an unworkable system without a new social drive such as the communists have managed to give it" . . .
It is a curious thing that here is one of the leading socialists in Britain who practically says it is no good unless they can import something of the communist attitude. On the other hand you get a man like Gordon Walker, who was a member of the last cabinet, and he is all in favour of more and more regimentation. He says:
Since the state is the main organ of authority in society, one of the natural ends of the new state will be to secure the increased quantum of authority necessary for the increased output of social energy ... In large part ... it will achieve this end by an extension of its positive functions; there will not be a village, a street or a house into which the new state does not enter, exacting respect for regulations, requiring information and rational action.
