It may amuse hon. members, but it has been suggested here that if we are going to guarantee those who lend money we ought to guarantee those who borrow money. That has been suggested. I thought first of all that it was a joke, but apparently it was not a joke.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that I am coming very near to the end of my time. I wish that somehow I could convince hon. members who are going to sit on this committee, and the people of Canada, that these extraordinary powers are not all necessary. I feel that what is needed is not a further extension of socialist powers, government powers, but the effort to bring freedom and private enterprise more into action as I think could have been done here if the attempt had been made.
I quoted what the hon. member for Eglin-ton said last week, and I should like to quote one or two more things from this book by Mr. Russell Kirk. In my opinion we should try to assess these things very carefully and not merely take some easy way to get an

During the remaining half of the present century, the principal endeavour of intelligent conservatives is likely to be resistant to the idea of a planned society, through restoration of an order which will make the planned society unnecessary and impracticable.
He goes on to say:
If, by the year 1984, justice, liberty and hope still are general characteristics of western social thought, the credit for this conservation of traditional values may belong to the school of genuinely reformatory and critical conservatism which is a growing influence in America and Britain . . .

speechtext:
I am at a loss to understand why he should think the bill would appeal to socialists, and equally at a loss to understand why he objects to it so strenuously from the corner in which he sits. Here we have a bill apparently designed to do nothing but protect the interests of the lending institutions, with which I have always understood my hon. friend had connections.
Let us see what the purposes of the government were in introducing the legislation. They are stated as being the promotion of the construction of new houses, the repair and modernization of existing houses and the improvement of housing and living conditions. They are worthy motives, but I wonder whether, after a year of operation of this legislation, the minister will not find himself perhaps murmuring the old tag, "How doth desire outrun performance".
I am giving him the credit, of course, of thinking that he has the desire to see houses built for the people of Canada. Let us take his own figures. An individual who is going to build an $8,000 house first of all has to find $800 for his down payment. He then has to buy a lot. I presume he will pay at least $200 for his lot. This is of course, Mr. Speaker, always assuming that today one can build a house for $8,000.
Here is our prospective buyer who now has to find a total of $1,000. Where will we find him in the population of Canada? I have the taxation statistics of the Department of National Revenue for 1953 covering the income brackets of all those taxable and nontaxable persons in Canada who filed income tax returns. We have those persons with incomes of under $1,000 who amount to 14-7 per cent of the total. I think the minister will agree with me that a person with an income of under $1,000 is not going to be able to find $1,000 for a down payment. So they are wiped out. The next group is persons with incomes between $1,000 and $2,000, and they amount to 28-1 per cent of our total population. Again I think the minister will agree with me when I say it is very dubious whether people with incomes of $2,000 or less are going to be able to find $1,000 for a down payment. Then we come to persons with incomes between $2,000 and $3,000. These amount to 30-4 per cent of the population.
This makes a total of 73 per cent of our population with incomes of less than $3,000 a year. I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that anyone with an income of $3,000 or less is

not going to be able to take advantage of this act. Someone has suggested that perhaps they are not eligible, that perhaps they do not fall into that quaint category the minister mentioned the other day when he referred to credit-worthy individuals. It struck me at the time that that was a rather curious form of worthiness.
Just to show how impractical is the suggestion that people of modest income are going to be able to build houses under the terms of this legislation, I should like to tell the house of what I saw in the state of California only a few months ago. In September I visited the peninsula south of San Francisco, probably one of the richest areas in North America. It is one vast garden all the way down from that city. All along the skyline boulevard highway private building developments are in progress. One may see large billboards advertising the terms upon which people may take advantage of what these builders have to offer. They are advertising houses to a value of $16,000 which can be obtained with a down payment of $400.
I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that that is a practical realization on the part of these private building contractors that the average family that aims to live in even a $16,000 house has very little cash to make a down payment. I have yet to hear any convincing argument which satisfies me as to the necessity for this down payment at all. We are told, of course, that it creates an interest in the property, and unless a down payment is made the purchaser will not care for the property after he gets it.
That seems to be a dubious argument. I believe that persons who are putting aside each month regular sums in the hope that they will own their homes some day will look after them whether down payments are made or not. The down payment requirement in this legislation makes it of practically no use to the people of Canada.
One of the great shortcomings in the bill is that there is no real provision for low rental housing to meet the needs of those people who cannot afford to pay the rentals charged today. There is of course a provision to aid private contractors in the building of multiple dwelling units, but this will not meet the needs of those in the low income brackets. It will meet the requirements of those in the middle and higher income brackets. I recall the sad experience many people had in Vancouver shortly after the war in dealing with Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. At that time apartment houses were erected, designed to accommodate veterans with children. First

of all the rents were to run between $40 and $50 a month. Those rents gradually crept up until they reached $60 or $70 a month.
That appears to be the situation in Ontario today. This past week end I was in Toronto visiting a young couple who are living in an apartment house constructed under the guarantee of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. They rent a small basement suite with a total floor area of between 600 and 700 square feet and pay $81 a month for this accommodation, and they have been told that when their lease expires the rent will increase to $100 a month.
These are conditions people in Canada are facing today. I might add that the young man in the case I have mentioned makes a weekly wage of just over $70. He told me when he went to that apartment he was obliged to pay three months' rent in advance. I presume this was to be a form of insurance against damage that can be done to an apartment. It is clearly just another racket; that is all it is, because there are terms in the lease saying that the owner can expend the whole of the advance to redecorate the apartment when the tenant moves out. In order to make this down payment of three months' rental at $81 a month this young man was obliged to go to a bank and sign a note to borrow the money. They are not a particularly extravagant couple, and have two small children. It is obvious that $70 a week is not enough to provide the thousand dollars required to take advantage of this legislation.
I am wondering what the purpose of this legislation is. The government has brought it in with a fine fanfare, stating that it is to promote the construction of new houses, the repair and modernization of existing houses and the improvement of housing and living conditions. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that it is nothing more or less than a cruel hoax being perpetrated upon the people of Canada by this government.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak my first few words in parliament inspired by the tremendous importance of this legislation and, particularly, its importance to my own constituency. York-Humber is a pulsating, growing suburban part of Toronto. Residential sections seem to spring up almost overnight. Young people are pouring in and, as in so many other urban parts of Canada, housing has become of vital importance to us.
This bill provides some relief, some assistance, to potential home owners; but there are thousands of people who will find no relief in it whatsoever. For instance, in my riding there are hundreds of young couples living under conditions of two and three families
National Housing Act
in a house, or living with their in-laws and in a shockingly overcrowded state. They have had to do this, not because they are unemployed or are incapable of maintaining homes. In many cases the wife as well as the husband is working, and each is drawing a quite reasonable salary; but they simply cannot make this down payment that must be made in the purchase of these houses. They cannot set aside that percentage of income required to secure a loan under the National Housing Act.
As I said, the wives as well as the husbands are working. I understand that under the regulations it is not possible to use their combined salaries; yet it seems to me that where a husband and wife are both working toward a common goal, the purchase of a home, they are really a better risk than is a husband with a higher salary whose wife is at home, with plenty of time on her hands to spend his money.
This bill will do nothing for the young people in the riding I represent. The attitude, which amounts almost to scorn, that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation seems to show for the small-salaried worker, and the even greater scorn it shows for a wife's earning capacity, makes it quite impossible for these young people to benefit by this legislation.
As the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Hees) said last Friday, under this new measure a prospective home owner must be receiving an income of $3,860 a year before he can apply for a National Housing Act loan. Well, there are many thousands of prospective home owners in my constituency who are certainly not earning even $3,000 a year. Among some of those couples, as I mentioned previously, the wives are also wage earners and their combined incomes would qualify them for a loan. I submit, sir, that wives' earnings, or at least a part of them, should be included in the amount that qualifies for a loan.
There is no doubt about it, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is one of the government's most successful arms of bureaucracy. I understand the losses under C.M.H.C. are practically nil, but so are the chances the corporation takes. Bureaucracy can always be successful because it takes no chances. I say, Mr. Speaker, that that is not the way this country was built, and at this stage in our growth it seems to me that such regimentation as is shown in this bill could stultify any further growth. Central Mortgage sits in its ivory tower here in Ottawa laying down the rules without any regard *for the drive and initiative of the individual.

National Housing Act
What I find suspect in this bill is the fact that there is one rule, and that one rule debars the small wage earner and also the average wage earner; so that while promising so much on the surface, in reality this bill could strangle housing for the majority of the people.
We all know the important part that Canadian banks played in building the Canadian west. In those days, unlike bureaucracy, the banks did take chances on the human element as well as on cold, hard cash. During the early days of this twentieth century, Canadian banks sent young men out to the prairies and over the Rockies to open up new branches for them. They were men of vision and imagination, and they were given much more power than bankers seem to have today. They were permitted to judge a man by his character as much as by the security he could offer when he was seeking a loan. Sometimes the borrowers on the prairie, the farmers, would have to borrow three times before they could pay back the amount. They would come again and again to the bank manager with a story of a bad crop, and then a bumper crop would come along and they would pay off the whole loan. If those prairie farmers had to show that they earned $3,000 a year before they were allowed a loan, well, the prairies would still be pretty arid and the west a bit of wilderness.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, this country has been built by men of vision and imagination, and not by bureaucrats in Ottawa who lay down one rule and take no chances whatever on human drive and initiative. I suggest that this bill should be expanded so it will give assistance to the average Canadian who wants a home of his own. The percentage of income required is too high.
I agree with one hon. member who asked why the government should say, in a country that is free, that a man has to have so much and spend so much on the maintenance of his home. Some people want to spend more on their homes than others. The down payments are too high, and in that regard I was interested in listening to the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Cameron) pointing out to us what private enterprise can do in San Francisco where they can build houses to sell for $16,000 and ask only a down payment of $400. I do not see why private enterprise could not do that here in Canada also.
A great Conservative prime minister, Benjamin Disraeli, once said that the social happiness of the millions should be the chief concern of a statesman. Well, I believe the home is the greatest of all social happiness. The very word "home" is a beautiful one to
[Miss Aitken.)
our Canadian ears, and I say that no government should debar the average or the small-salaried Canadian from owning his own home.

maintopic: SUBSTITUTION OF NEW LEGISLATION TO INSURE APPROVED LENDERS, ETC.
speechtext:
I want to compliment the hon. member who has just taken her seat on her very able and relaxed effort in her first address in this house. With much of what she had to say I agree, but there is a spot or two where we might disagree with her. However, at this time I am not going to do it, not until she has had a better chance of looking over this forum and perhaps revising her opinion.
I would just like to say that the great difficulty in the part of the country from which I come-and it is still operated, mind you, under the free enterprise system-is not getting homes at the present time but keeping the people in the homes they have established over the years. That is our main problem. I want to suggest that the cure for lack of housing in Canada is not slogans.
I was rather disappointed in the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell). He is always very fair and inclined to be factual; but when he gets up in the house, takes a book and reads the title, and judging by what he quoted from it, it was very appropriate, and pulls a few sentences out of their context-and you know how prone the Americans are at this time to eulogize anything going on in Britain-and give it to the house as the opinion of G. D. H. Cole on a certain subject, all I can say is that I am reasonably sure that if the whole article by Cole were quoted the house would get an entirely different impression. However, that is by the way.
As I see this question, Mr. Speaker, it is tied up with a lot of other matters to which we have to give consideration. Since 1945 this world has been going through a process of change. In my judgment it is a complete revolution that affects the whole world. There are no guideposts to lead us along the way. It is one world today. We have been going through this cold war process. In the cold war, in my opinion, the thing that stands out to a greater extent than developing armies and guns has been the advice we have received from time to time from people who were in a position to give us that advice: that the social and economic conditions of North America particularly are more important to us than the development of armies.
The system in North America is on trial as far as China, Africa and other countries we refer to as backward are concerned. They look to us, and they judge the system that we

represent on the basis of how we do our housekeeping and how we take care of the people who live under that system. In the social and economic structure of this country the thing that stands out in my judgment as a first and must is the housing of our people.
If we are successful in preventing a shooting war, and it looks as though we will be, then the thing we have to do is develop an objective in this country toward which we can take our people. We united ourselves during the war. We had a common objective in defeating fascism. The people got behind us to help win that war and we now have to answer the questions asked, not only by the men who were in the services but by those who were in the plants and factories. They ask, what were we fighting for? They contend that they were fighting for the right to retain what they had and to go forward into something better. There are hundreds of thousands of those veterans who do not forget the slogans on which we fought the last war.
As I said, one of the first things is housing our people. I do not think you can develop good citizenship in any country until you give the individual citizen a stake in that country, a piece of land, a home which he owns, the right to say, "This little bit of Canada is mine; I have something to fight for." If we said now that we were going to declare war on slums, that we were going to give our people the right to own homes in so far as their ability will enable them to do so; if we made that an objective for the Canadian people and told them that we were going to spend some money in the future in that way as we have been spending it on war, then I think we would at least be living up to some of the promises made during the days of the shooting war when the world was threatened, and when we felt we were fighting for something better.
The Chinaman, the African and people in other backward countries are looking to North America as the last bastion of democracy as we know it. We had better smarten up and try to fix it up in order to give them an incentive to strive in their own countries for something similar to what we have in Canada.
I am disappointed in the bill, and for this reason. In 1945 the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) tabled a white paper in this house. One of the things stressed on several pages-if anyone wants to have a look at it I would refer them to pages 3, 10 and 11-was housing. That was one of the things pointed out definitely by the white paper. There was going to be a program
National Housing Act
managed by the government that would enable returning service personnel to get homes of their own. The people of Canada were going to get housing generally better than it was previous to the war.
In that white paper the government outlined what their future policy was in regard to the whole development of Canada. Step by step they pointed out that free enterprise would have the right to develop the country and work on the resources, but they also gave a warning that where free enterprise failed to fill the bill the government would step in and supplement their efforts. That is what the government has failed to do in the matter of housing particularly.
The hon. member who spoke just before me made reference to the fact that in the United States free enterprise had been able to build houses for a certain figure, as indicated by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Cameron). She wanted to know why Canada could not do the same thing. If the hon. member takes a look at the whole picture she will find that United States capital is doing a lot of things in Canada that you cannot get Canadian capital to do. I would refer to the development of our iron ore and so forth. United States capital is coming into this country and working on our resources because Canadians who have capital apparently either have not the initiative or the courage to put their money into any project that is all-Canadian. The Americans are gamblers. They are ready to get out and do things, and that is why you can get houses in the United States much easier and at cheaper rates than in Canada. Apparently our people who have money are afraid to spend it, or they have not much confidence in the future of Canada.
My No. 1 disagreement is that the government announced a very good policy in 1945 in their white paper with particular reference to housing. The bill which the minister has brought in falls far short of living up to the announcement made at that time that where free enterprise failed-and it has failed completely in providing the Canadian people with homes-the government would step in and see that they were provided with homes. This bill does not do that.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when we recessed for dinner I was making a few observations

National Housing Act
on Bill No. 102 amending the National Housing Act, and I was emphasizing that the policy and philosophy of the government, as laid down in their white paper in 1945, was not being followed in so far as housing is concerned. They laid down a very good policy at that time, but unfortunately they have not followed their own program. In that document tabled in April, 1945, they said that in the National Housing Act, as in all other matters affecting the economic future of Canada, they would depend on the system of free enterprise to do the job, but that where free enterprise fell down the government would step in and supplement what they were not able to do. In the matter of housing that has not happened.
There is no doubt that since 1945 the people of Canada have not been provided with houses under the system of free enterprise. From 1945 on, previous to the amendments, the National Housing Act was largely in the hands of the insurance companies in Canada. They had a lot of money invested, but they certainly did not provide the Canadian people with homes. In fact if you check the figures closely you will find that the backlog of housing that existed seven or eight years ago has not yet been caught up with. We have to a large extent met the demand created since that time, but I believe I am safe in saying there is a backlog of housing in Canada today of around 400,000 family units. That still has to be taken care of; and if you take the natural increase we can expect, and couple that with the fact that the Minister of Immigration and Citizenship (Mr. Harris) announced a few weeks ago that the government planned in 1954 to bring into Canada an additional 168,000 new citizens who will have to find themselves places to live, then the mechanics of this new bill are, in my judgment, not going to meet the need.
To begin with let us have a look at the drawbacks. The bill itself may provide housing for those in the higher income brackets and for some in the middle class, but it definitely will not provide housing for those on average incomes in Canada. There is one group who are not going to be able to get houses on a home ownership basis under this bill. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), when he brought down his last budget, in discussing the tax rates told us in this house that there were 137,000 families in Canada on incomes below the taxable level. That was families, mind you, and families require houses. That group below the income tax level will not be able to build or rent houses under the arrangements provided in the amendments to the National Housing Act. They are out.

Second, those on average incomes-and the average is under $3,000 for the majority of wage and salary earners in Canada-will also be unable to take advantage of this bill. Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation determine what they call an "economic unit" which is around $10,080 with a lending value of $12,000, and they also insist on an income of around $3,800 a year. There is no point in the average wage earner, earning under $3,000 or around that figure per year, applying for a loan under this bill. He cannot meet income requirements and therefore he is out. You can add that large group to the 137,000 families with incomes under the income tax level.
Looking at the bill on that basis you are not going to provide houses for 10 per cent of the people of this country. The test of income and the "economic unit" as defined by the bill at the present time automatically disqualify them. So we are just wasting our time if we think this bill is going to provide homes for average Canadians.

Another matter the government was lax in supervising, not only the federal government but the provincial and municipal governments also, was that of land speculation, which is one of the main stumbling blocks today in the provision of homes.
Take any city or town across Canada of any size and take a look at values of land back in 1945 and beyond that, then take a look at what you have to pay for a lot in these towns and cities today, and you will find that the average person on an average income cannot even afford to buy a lot. I am told, though 1 would not swear to this, that there are lots in this city today that cost around $8,000. People who were smart, anticipating what is happening today, namely that the government would take some responsibility in the matter of housing, got hold of land in and around towns and cities across Canada and they are now holding on to it. Today they are holding a gun

to the heads of those who need houses, and in that way we are left with the major problem of finding land for the average person who may want to own a house in or around a town or city of any size in the Dominion of Canada.
I think something should have been done a long time ago, though I believe perhaps we are too late now, with regard to people holding land for speculative purposes. Theirs, I think, was a very unpatriotic act.
A load has been dumped on the municipalities. If one undertakes a housing development in any of the municipalities and towns across Canada today, we find the town is left with the responsibility of servicing the land, and most of the towns and cities today are pretty well up against it in the matter of finances. The larger cities, of course, where they have a lot of property, are not quite so badly off but in most of the smaller towns the situation is not quite so good regarding the servicing of land.
Under the present bill the rate of interest has not been fixed, but the minister did suggest the other day it might run around 6 per cent.

I would not quibble over a
fraction. I suggested around 6 per cent. The banks are going to be protected. They are going to benefit by that interest rate. They are going to be insured. They are not taking any chances. That is not free enterprise. There is no risk capital there. The taxpayers of Canada are guaranteeing it.
Under this act everybody is protected except the man who purchases a home. They are guaranteed by the taxpayers of Canada against any loss of any kind; but under the insurance scheme laid down by the act the purchaser of a home has no protection whatsoever. A man who undertakes to make the down payment obligates himself for the amount of the mortgage. He may continue to make his regular instalments for ten years, and may get some equity in the property. Then he may take sick or lose his job and be obliged to move to another part of the country. He is not able to handle the payments on that property any longer, or maybe he is not permitted to live in the house. He has to get out and find other ways and means of providing that he may eat. The bank is insured. It is not going to lose anything. But for the property holder, who has perhaps put $2,000, $3,000 or $4,000 into the property, there is no insurance whatever.

He could buy it.
National Housing Act

Most of those people would be in a nice position to buy it, if they could not make their payments. That is why the man has to get out, or why he has to go to some other part of the country. He has no insurance whatsoever. Whatever equity he has in that property is gone, but the poor little bank is to be protected to the extent of about 90 per cent by the taxpayers of Canada. That is not right. It is immoral, in my judgment, and is something that should be corrected.
We are not asking the government to go into the housing business in Canada for the purpose of stimulating the profits of either the insurance companies or the banks. That is not the objective. The objective is or should be that of getting homes for the people of this country so they may become citizens of the country with a stake in it and be able to say with pride, "I own something in this country besides a place in which to bury me when I pass away". If you are looking for initiative, incentive or that kind of thing, may I say that I think some of the guarantees and protection given to the moneylenders should be given to the purchaser of the property who is endeavouring to make a contribution to the country and to obtain citizenship status.
I think perhaps the interest rate is the biggest stumbling block in connection with the whole matter. My own personal view is that we shall never provide houses for the people of this country on the basis on which we are attempting to do it at the present time. As I said a moment ago, that group of 137,000 families is out as far as this act is concerned, and the large percentage of salaried workers across Canada earning an income of about $3,000 are also out. They are not going to get any housing under this particular act in the form in which we are discussing it at the present time. In their last presentation to the government on December 10, 1953 the Canadian Congress of Labour placed the emphasis where it belonged, in my opinion; because the average person in Canada today, at present prices, cannot afford to become a home owner under the National Housing Act. In a memorandum to the government the Canadian Congress of Labour touched on the whole question of housing and in their final summing up they had this to say:
. . . very few Canadian workers can afford to build their own homes.
Assuming, as conservative expert opinion does, that a wage earner should not buy a home costing more than 2i times his annual income, and taking eight heavy industries (coal mining, metal mining, pulp and paper mills, heavy electrical apparatus, primary iron and steel, motor vehicles, non-ferrous metal smelting and refining, and products of petroleum and coal) in which most of the workers are full-grown men, we find that in only

National Housing Act one of the eight are wage earners now getting enough to buy even the cheapest type of N.H.A. house. And these are the high-wage industries.
The most urgent need is for low-rental housing. This means subsidized public housing. The government has provided for this, in section 35 of the act. But it is doing little or nothing to make the section known, let alone promote it, in the local communities which have to take the initiative in bringing it into operation.
I think the Canadian Congress of Labour, who have their finger on the pulse of the industrial workers of this country anyway, stressed the essential point under present circumstances when they pinpointed the question of low rental housing. As they point out in their memorandum, section 35 of the National Housing Act does now make provision, in co-operation with provincial governments, for the application of low-rental housing.
In what position are the provincial governments to take advantage of that section of the act? Some of them may be in a position to do so. Ontario may be in a position to take advantage of it, and Quebec to some extent, and British Columbia; but the maritime provinces are not in this position. Where the federal government offers either to match dollar for dollar with them, as in connection with the health grants, or even on the 75-25 per cent basis, the provincial governments with low incomes are not in a position to embark on any kind of program that means any large outlay of capital which is to be tied up for any considerable period of time. They could not take advantage of it.
I agree with the criticism made by the congress of labour in that memorandum, to the effect that this section of the act has never been stressed, has never been pushed as it should have been, that the use that could have been made of it has not been made, and that it is not a solution. As indicated in the memorandum of the Canadian Congress of Labour, the scheme might have to be subsidized; and money should be made available to the municipalities which have to service the land, at a rate of interest not greater than 2 per cent. A special fund should be set up to be administered by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, and the money should be made available directly to the municipalities, cutting out all the middlemen in between, in order that the municipalities which are in a position to do so may be able to embark upon a housing program designed by themselves to take care of their own needs in accordance with the planning they may have done for expansion, the building of their towns and the servicing of their land. That is not a new suggestion. That was done back in the twenties. I can show


you groups of houses that were built under a plan similar to that back in the twenties after the first war. They were good, substantial houses. I never heard about any trouble in getting the rents. They were all paid for. Those who went into those houses on a rental plan ultimately became owners of those properties. They are all owned privately now, but in the first place they were built by the municipalities in that way. In my judgment the Canadian government is not going to be able to fulfil its obligation to the Canadian people, with present prices and circumstances, in any other way.
Then I do not think the federal government has done enough advertising with respect to the assistance that can be had by co-operative organizations in the building of homes, and their recognition in the act as lending institutions. In Nova Scotia we have a provincial co-operative housing act. It has been in effect for some considerable time and I think it is one of the best acts of its kind in Canada. The only drawback has been that funds have not been available to make it work. If the minister could arrive at an arrangement under this legislation-

Some person may say that this plan is going to be a wonderful thing because the local bank manager who knows the needs of the people is going to be able to sit down in his own town, his own community, and determine whether or not John Jones should get a loan for housing. After he has compiled that information he will send the applications to the head office in Montreal, and they will be sent back with a red pencil mark through them. Head office will say that the economic future of that part of the country is not good enough to warrant the investment of any of their money over a period of 25 or 30 years.

There is such a place as "Jesse James" street down there. We have to overcome the complicated, mysterious, administrative roadblocks that have caused trouble in housing since at least 1945.
The minister comes from Nova Scotia. I suggest to him that money should be made available at a reasonable rate of interest directly to co-operative groups under the Nova Scotia housing act. Their legislation is properly administered, and they are easy people to talk to. They have done a lot of building so far, and there has never been a suggestion that anyone has ever defaulted on payments. There has never been any trouble, and they have provided many good substantial homes at reasonable rates. If you can cut out the red tape of the banks and the insurance companies and make money available to these co-operative groups at proper rates of interest you will not have any trouble in that area with regard to housing.

be done in providing houses this year as was done under the old act last year, even with the insurance companies. I think less money is going to be available. The banks will administer things on a much more conservative basis, and we are going to wind up at the end of 1954 with a much bigger backlog in housing than we have at the present time.
I think it was a proper step to make section 35 complementary to the Nova Scotia cooperative housing act, and the only thing wrong now is the rate of interest. If you can succeed in lowering it and make money available throughout the provinces of Canada to provide low rental housing you are going to take care of a large group of wage and salary earners who will never get houses under the National Housing Act by applying to the banks. You will also help to provide low rental housing for the 137,000 families mentioned by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) who live on incomes below the income tax level. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill now before the house has given us once more the opportunity of hearing the sempiternal jeremiads, criticisms and lamentations of the opposition. The way our Conservative friends speak, one would think that they have the monopoly of kindness towards the people! It is so true that were we not conversant with their past, their extremely revealing past, we might be led to believe them when they seem to take an interest in the low wage earners. But we know that the government can never do anything to please Her Majesty's loyal opposition. If we gave them the moon, I believe they would ask for Mars, if not Venus, and would want still more.
It is quite easy to criticize a party in power. But one should make worth-while suggestions to improve the situation.
Some C.C.F. members, and in particular, I believe, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) suggested that the rate of interest should be 2 per cent with amortization spread over a 40-year period. Well, why not go further and ask the government to pay a premium to all who wish to become

National Housing Act
home owners? We must take a realistic view of the situation and recognize what the government has done for housing up to now.
Going back to the years where no help of that kind was to be expected from the government, the best mortgage a prospective home owner could hope for was 50 per cent of the amount he was ready to invest. Today the amount has been raised to 90 per cent, 80 per cent of the first $8,000 and 70 per cent of the amount above $8,000, which means that with a down payment of $1,400, one can build a $10,000 house, thanks to the government. I do not bring any new facts. I am just reviewing the main sections of the bill before making my own deductions.
Really I wonder if in ordinary business today you could obtain an $8,600 loan on a $10,000 property? That is impossible. You might have the greatest reputation in the world but nobody in business would be willing to transact anything on that basis. So that is one step better than what the government has so far given us.
The opposition has made much of the fact that to take advantage of this legislation a man had to earn between $3,500 and $3,860 a year. I know, of course, that those who have no special skills do not at present earn this salary but I do not think I am wrong in saying that all skilled tradesmen earn at least $3,500 a year, if not more, so that a large number of those whose revenue is $3,500 or more are in a position to benefit from this offer on the government's part.
Now, you will say that the government should have given more thought to those whose revenue is less than $3,500. Of course one can always do better and the more the government will do to encourage home ownership, the more they will deserve the praise of the interested parties. Still, while I feel sorry for those whose earnings are less than $3,500 a year, I do feel, Mr. Speaker, that I am in a very good position to deal with this matter. As it is, the people in my constituency are workers, and, for the most part, skilled craftsmen, the rest being what are commonly called helpers, or day labourers.
I would like each of them to own a house. I would like all of them to benefit from other generosities of the government and own a house. But we cannot do everything at once. However, it is possible that we may be

advancing toward the goal desired by each and every one of us. It has been said-it is not I who said it, and I do not rejoice at the thought-that, unfortunately, there will always be poor people among us. There will always be people who will not be able to afford to own a house; there were such people in the past, and it will be the same in the future. It is inevitable. It is a situation that we must accept, but we must try to improve it for the working classes, those who earn less than $3,500. They are protected by unemployment insurance, by family allowances and in various other ways, but we ought to study their case in order that they may benefit from the facilities which are being provided under this bill.
Formerly, when the small wage earner wished to become a home owner, every member of the family would get together in order to contribute to a common fund, and the savings of everyone would be sufficient for a down payment on a house. Well, I fail to see how things are different today, for it is still possible to achieve the same result through the same means. Every member of the family can help the head of that family, who has made great sacrifices, who has saved quite a bit, not only to make both ends meet but also to make his dream come true, that is to own a house of his own. Well, I would imagine that by saving wisely, one can make such a dream come true even today!
Mr. Speaker, there are some who think they are furthering the interests of the country when they claim that our citizens cannot benefit from the proposed legislation because their income is too low. Our provincial governments and our municipalities also have responsibilities in that field; they must accept them and use the facilities which the proposed legislation will offer as they could use in the past the facilities offered under the existing act, which enabled our municipalities and our provinces to build dwellings to replace existing slums and unhealthy houses. There is a provision in another act for that purpose, which was underlined by the minister in the following words:
.	. . Or where a municipality and a province
feel there is need for rental accommodation with subsidized rentals for families of low income, the federal government will participate to the extent of 75 per cent of the capital investment and subsequent operating losses. Where slum clearance and housing redevelopment are desirable, federal participation is available for 50 per cent of the cost of the slum clearance.

Those who have complained about the scarcity of houses have never hoped that one day everyone would own his own house, but all have wished that conditions might become such that families could house themselves without having to crowd into dwellings that are too small. When we succeed, through this bill, in increasing the number of houses available in the country, we will enable people who now have to share housing accommodation to occupy premises vacated by the owners of new houses. Again I say that everyone cannot become a home owner.
As I stated before, one must remember that provincial and municipal governments also have their share of responsibility in that field. Besides, provincial governments now have sufficient revenues. For instance, if we examine the budget of the province of Quebec, we find that it now stands at $308 million, while between 1930 and 1934 its revenue was approximately $52 million. I believe it might be possible to take advantage of this plan to undertake a housing program of dwellings suitable for two or three people only. Here again another great problem arises. It is not simply a matter of building five or six-room dwellings, as in the case of those who would avail themselves of this plan to build $6,000 or $8,000 houses. I am wondering how we shall proceed when the provincial government decides to embark on a large-scale building program to supply homes for those who have none. Houses will have to be built for the large number of families who are today living in hovels that are detrimental to the moral as well as the physical well-being of our fellow citizens.
Well, that legislation will enable us to lay the foundations for such a program and I hope that it will be implemented in the near future for the benefit of the whole population.
Now, some hon. members have contended that the monthly payments to be met by the home owner under this program are too high. I have always understood, and those who have kept themselves somewhat informed about economic conditions in this country have always thought that a month's rent should be the equivalent of a week's earnings. Well, on the basis of the revenue of a home owner taking advantage of this plan, we see that his monthly rent will not exceed his weekly earnings, as the amortization of 83276-91J
National Housing Act
his debt, spread over a period of 25 or 30 years, will entail payments of only $58 to $60 per month.
Those payments are by no means excessive. The government are not acting with undue haste but they are going along slowly and wisely, meeting new situations as they arise in this country. That is what we must look forward to. There is no need for us to be ashamed as we rise to support a measure such as that which is being introduced here at this time by the government. They are not rushing into this madly, they are not losing their heads over the situation but are wisely looking over matters.
No one can seriously imply, not even my C.C.F. friends, that there might come a time when property owners who have taken advantage of this plan will lose the money they have spent because they will no longer be able to meet their obligations.
Now, gentlemen, that is easy to say, and it is very easy to appear to sympathize with the plight of the poor. But, as far back as I can remember, I have known that those who cannot meet their obligations unfortunately stand to lose, in many instances, what they have already paid. Such is the case for automobiles, electric refrigerators and so on. If the buyer is not in a position to meet his payments, he stands to lose what he has already paid. That is unfortunate, but he must accept his loss, as we all have to accept our woes, since we are all in a valley of tears, as it is so well put in a certain prayer.
The government has made things easier, perhaps not for everybody, but at least for 90 per cent of those who will now wish to become home owners, and I am sure that they will all be in a position to meet their obligations. Even if the prospective homeowner under one of those plans became so ill as to lose his job, the remainder of his family would still be there, able to come to his help. I hope that enough of the old family spirit has survived to inspire them to do their share to avert the disaster, even at the price of great sacrifices. I dare hope that our fellow Canadians have kept enough of that family spirit to come to the help of their parents, in such circumstances. There should not be too many cases of foreclosure of mortgages, and I hope that such cases will never arise.

National Housing Act
Some have tried to minimize the advantages from which people will benefit now that banks are allowed to grant mortgage loans. I know very well that the humble manager of the branch around the corner will not have authority to make a decision in all cases but his influence will make itself felt in the main office. Here I am thinking especially of the city of Montreal and the surrounding district. Now at the same time this will put an end to a situation that was truly deplorable for certain citizens of our metropolis, more particularly in certain districts east and southwest of Montreal where lending companies refused to lend money pretending that it was economically unsound to do so in that part of the country, because the security factor prevented them from lending money in the districts I have just mentioned. Well, banks having branches in the various parts of our city and wishing to do business throughout the city of Montreal will be able at any time to recommend to their head office the loans requested in their respective districts, so that all parts of Montreal will be on an equal footing.
Now, it has been said that it is quite probable that no more than 100,000 dwellings can be built. I am no expert in the matter, but I am wondering, Mr. Speaker, whether we have sufficient manpower and skilled labour to build more than 100,000 houses in the same year. Like everyone else, we hope that the housing crisis will soon end. However, one must not be too optimistic about the possible results of the bill now before the house. I hope that it may enable us to remedy the situation as soon as possible. If I said that we can find in the country sufficient labour to remedy the situation in one year, my colleagues might be tempted to take my remarks jokingly. It will undoubtedly take some years before that can be done. But legislation of this kind will enable a large proportion of our people to become home owners, to build houses of their own.
I could dwell longer on the matter, but I will limit my remarks to the interest rate. It is true that anyone can personally seek information from loan companies, or from the banks to find out what the interest rate would be on a first mortgage loan. I believe that it would not be easy to obtain such a loan at less than 6 per cent. I hope that the rate will not reach 6 per cent and that it will be set between 5 and 6 per cent and even lower

if possible, though I don't think that it is feasible.
It is easy perhaps to wish that the rate be set at 2 per cent. If those who advocate such a rate were in power, they would be the first to admit that it is impossible to set the interest rate much below 6 per cent. I do not question their sincerity. They want our fellow citizens to benefit from a 3 or 3J per cent and even 3J per cent reduction in the interest rate. If our friends opposite want a 2 per cent interest rate there is nothing to prevent them from making representations to the authorities of their respective provinces in order to get them to undertake to pay the difference between the likely rate of 6 per cent and the 2 per cent rate suggested by the opposition. As I see it, their suggestion has no other purpose but to lure the people with bright prospects. As far as we are concerned, we have here a bill the results of which will surely be beneficial to a great number of our fellow citizens.
That is why, Mr. Speaker, I do not hesitate to give my wholehearted support to this measure. I express the hope that this government may keep on improving the situation, through a policy which is so beneficial to those who wish to become home owners. It is possible that the government may be in a position to do better in the not far distant future and I hope that they will take advantage of every opportunity to do good in all fields under their jurisdiction.

Mr. Speaker, at this stage in the debate there is a tendency for discussion to become somewhat repetitious. I think that is all to the good, because I feel that the subject of housing in Canada is one of the most important topics that members of this house could discuss. I say that not merely because of the debate we have had during the past three days and the inspiration derived from listening to the various speeches, but also because of a keen personal interest I have had in this topic for the past seven or eight years since the war.
My close personal interest in this subject arises first because I belong to the age category which has felt most severely the postwar pressure on housing in Canada. I remember vividly my own experience of venturing into housing in the manner to which so many young couples have had to resort these days, by subletting a few rooms in a home. The

demand for a private home soon became imperative. My first investigations into the subject were carried on in 1947, when I discussed the matter with real estate men who were supposed to have an intimate knowledge of the real estate situation in Canada. Their advice was that houses were at the top level of value. They suggested that on the basis of their experience I should wait until such time as prices would level off, when I would be able to purchase housing accommodation on a more permanent basis and for a more equitable value.
That was in 1947. In 1948 the price of houses soared another $1,000. In 1949 it went up further. By the time I finally took upon myself a house I found that I could have saved some $2,000 or $3,000 had I taken advantage of the opportunity back in 1947. I found also that even though I had managed to save a fairly substantial sum of money in order to make a down payment, it was not adequate to meet the requirements of the National Housing Act at that time and I had to assume a double mortgage.
As I say, I have had a personal interest in this subject along with a large number of Canadians in the same age category as myself. I remember taking part in a discussion back in 1949, a year or so before I came to this house. We used to get together in a citizens' forum discussion group and one evening the topic discussed was "When do we get more houses?" As I have listened to this debate it seemed to me that that topic is just as pertinent today as it was in those days.
I recall carrying on an exchange of correspondence with the member who represented the old Brandon riding at that time, the late Mr. Matthews. He was interested in housing and we pursued the subject by correspondence for several weeks at the time the special amendments were being introduced, I believe in 1949. In a sense then I am merely expressing in this debate the interest and the emphasis of the members who in the past have represented the constituencies of Brandon and Souris in this House of Commons.
It has been said that, next to national defence, housing is the most important domestic problem in this country. Several hon. members have dealt with that particular aspect of the topic already during the debate, and have suggested that there are very serious social implications involved in housing. We have heard it said that if we solved our housing problem we might solve all the major social problems that are besetting the large urban communities during these complex post-war days.
National Housing Act
I am not going to oversimplify to that extent, because I do not think there is any one cause that can explain the problems of juvenile delinquency, broken homes, divorce, mental illness and those other difficulties that have been referred to here this afternoon. I do not accept the environmentalists' theory holus-bolus, neither do I believe that there is no major contribution to social well-being to be made by the provision of adequate housing.
I would like to point out that we should not confuse the issue. Merely providing a house does not necessarily mean that you are providing a home. There is a vast difference between a home and the physical facilities that would be provided in a house. The problem of establishing a home, and by that I mean a healthful, wholesome environment in which a family can grow up, in which children can be shaped into responsible citizenship in our twentieth century civilization, involves much more than the mere provision of the physical facilities. It involves a number of subtle spiritual and psychological factors.
I shall sum up this part of my speech by stating that I agree generally with the statement made by Phyllis Burns who, speaking as secretary of the Canadian Welfare Council's family welfare division-

And very appropriate, too.
I certainly think he had something worth while to say about housing and families. But whether Miss Burns is related to Rabbie Burns I do not know. However, she was reported in the Ottawa Citizen of May 2, 1952, as follows:
A lack of housing has become Canada's most acute social problem affecting family life, Phyllis Burns, secretary of the Canadian Welfare Council's family welfare division, said yesterday. More causes of family quarreling, desertions and juvenile delinquency have been traced to the housing scarcity than to any other cause, Miss Burns said. Her estimate was based on field reports by Canadian welfare agencies across the country.
We all highly respect the opinions of the Canadian Welfare Council because that group is very closely in touch with conditions in Canada generally so far as social problems are concerned.
The reason the housing situation in Canada has such serious social implications is that it is largely young couples, at the beginning of their family careers, who are affected. These young Canadian families from which will come the generations of the future will be moulded by the family atmosphere established in these young family groups, and that atmosphere will have a very serious bearing on the Canada of the future. Unfortunately it is these younger families who
143S

National Housing Act
are most seriously affected, and it is they who are least able to assume the financial obligation of obtaining a home, a reasonably adequate home, either by purchase or through rental.
Looking at the local situation for a moment, the city of Brandon is not a large city, certainly not among the largest cities in Canada, but in that community alone there are 150 young veterans still waiting to obtain accommodation in the group of wartime houses established in Brandon shortly after the war. I know this to be a fact because every time one of these houses becomes vacant I get the impression that I hear from the remaining 149 who did not get the vacant house, and they ask why they with their eligibility they did not obtain the house that became available.
In addition to the problem of the young couples we have the effect of the housing shortage on the group I might call senior citizens. I believe it is the senior citizens, the older age group in Canada at the present time, along with those who are just beginning their family careers, who are suffering most. These senior citizens have become victims in a society which has undergone the rapid changes which accompanied the industrial revolution. Canada has rapidly become urbanized, with the result that fathers and mothers, the pioneers who played their part in the foundation of this country, are being very hard-pressed to find suitable accommodation. The smaller families-and I think it is recognized that the family unit tends to be smaller on an average across Canada- are not able to care for grandmothers and grandfathers as they did when the majority of families lived on the farm. There is also the problem of increasing longevity. These two groups create a very urgent demand.
As I have listened to the debate during these past three days it has seemed to me we have viewed the problem slightly out of perspective. The emphasis has been on the urgent demand of the moment, but it seemed to me as the discussion proceeded that there has always been a housing shortage in Canada right from the early pioneering days. Here we must, I believe, make a distinction between real demand and real needs, because we know human needs can become insatiable. Human beings, so far as material and physical needs are concerned, have horizons which are unlimited; and in this day and age, when we emphasize materialistic values more perhaps than in the early pioneering period of Canada's development, it seems we are not as easily satisfied as our forefathers in regard
[Mr. Dinsdale.l
to housing. Perhaps the need is not much greater, but certainly there is a wider demand for better housing accommodation today.
The housing shortage is a problem of long standing because with the wave of immigration in the early part of this century, when 2 million people landed 'on Canadian shores in a relatively short period of time, hardly anything was done to provide suitable housing accommodation for the newcomers.
During the Christmas recess I read that very excellent biography of the late J. S. Woodsworth, and I was intrigued to learn that it was while he was serving in a mission in the north end of Winnipeg, and dealing with some of the housing and social difficulties created by this wave of immigrants pouring into our urban areas, that he first began to think in terms of political and economic action as a means of solving basic human problems rather than relying on religious emphasis as had formerly been the case. I do not want to oversimplify this, but it might well be that this housing crisis and the impact it had upon its founder gave rise to the C.C.F. movement in Canada. The wave of immigration, the shift of population to the urban areas, the industrial revolution, the resulting growth, and the tendency to build houses that degenerated very quickly into slums have all contributed to the confused political situation in which we find ourselves today.
There is a backlog in housing demand, not necessarily housing need, that has been estimated at anything from 100,000 to 700,000 housing' units. The matter came to a head during world war II, when for a period of four or five years there was hardly any housing construction at all, with the result that in 1944 the government had to take serious steps toward grappling with the backlog of demand. Since then increasing government attention has been given to housing in Canada and I noticed, as I reviewed the situation, that unfortunately the response to government measures and the results from these measures have not always been good.
There has been a somewhat disappointing result from the legislation thus far. That statement applies even to the legislation I referred to, namely that of 1949, when enabling legislation was passed by this house making it possible for the three levels of government-federal, provincial and municipal-to deal especially with the provision of low-rental units. That legislation seemed to offer an excellent solution to this difficulty which would relieve the pressure with regard to young couples to whom I have referred

and also with regard to older age groups. Unfortunately there have not been too many projects developed under this legislation. It seems to me this stalemate has resulted mainly because the legislation was only enabling legislation and its success depended on the initiative of the provincial and the municipal governments. In most cases this initiative has been lacking.
In Manitoba steps were taken in the legislature to make it possible to take advantage of the federal legislation, but that was just about as far as the matter went in our province. Individual schemes must be approved by plebiscite before the municipalities can proceed to meet the urgent need for low-cost and low-rental units. While the municipalities would like to do something about it, unfortunately they are not financially able to do so. They are hamstrung financially by a tax situation that is only too well known in this country. They cannot put up even the small percentage that is required of municipalities under section 35 of the National Housing Act. They cannot put up the money nor can they provide the serviced land necessary to deal with the situation.
As hon. members on all sides of the house are aware, the crux of this problem arises from the fact that the municipalities will never be able to cope with the situation financially until the main burden of providing for general services of health, welfare and education is shifted to the senior governments. We cannot expect taxes on property, which is the main source of municipal revenue, to handle these services. Actually municipalities can scarcely handle the demands for local services such as roads, sewers, sidewalks and so forth, let alone indulge in the luxury of providing the general services of health, welfare and education.
In reading my local paper, the Brandon Daily Sun, of last Friday, I believe it was, I was interested to note that one of the points stressed at the meeting of the Manitoba municipal association, the first major point to be stressed by the president, was this problem of the inequitable distribution of taxes and responsibilities among the three levels of government. This situation becomes especially difficult where there are no large industrial developments to supply broader tax resources for municipal purposes. This of course is true where you have an area that is made up of smaller rural communities or smaller urban areas. Unfortunately, as has been pointed out by many others who have taken part in this debate, the new legislation that we have before us will not begin to deal with this difficulty.
National Housing Act
To bring these remarks to a conclusion and generally to appraise the legislation in the light of the observations I have already made, may I say this. Even to keep up with current demands we need some 130,000 new housing units annually. This requirement has never been met under any of the legislation put forward by the government up to the present time, and it does not appear that we are going to be much better off under the new legislation.
On the surface it would seem that the basic problems of lower down payments, more readily available mortgage funds, and a longer period of amortization are going to be met; but as various hon. members have proceeded to analyse the legislation, it seems obvious to me that all these provisions are going to be invalidated by the fact that we are still faced with high costs of construction.
This was the problem that first beset me when I began to pursue some solution for my own housing difficulties; and it is still the basic problem that will largely invalidate the effectiveness of this legislation before us. It is not going to meet the situation where the urgent need is felt, namely among the younger families who tend to be in the lower income groups because they are starting out on their careers; and certainly it is not going to deal with the problem of low-cost housing for our older age group.
Various solutions have been put forward by hon. members, and I am not going to labour that point. This is merely a discussion preliminary to the legislation going to the committee. In that committee, as it continues the discussion, I trust that something will be done to deal with this problem that seems to be the central one, namely that of the cost of housing soaring beyond the capacity of the ordinary wage earner to meet it.
We have had the "co-op" housing scheme put forward as a solution. I concur in the suggestion that this scheme could help in a real way to deal with the difficulty in the lower-income group. We have also had the suggestion that we should eliminate some of the frills on the houses sponsored by the National Housing Act, so the cost might be kept low enough to enable advantage to be taken of the improved financial terms.
In the city of Brandon one contractor has been able to put up a series of homes priced at $7,200, which is just about the level that the ordinary young family is able to meet. But unfortunately, because these units do not meet the specifications of the National Housing Act, they are not covered by this kind of financing. That difficulty is also related to the fact that serviced land is not

National Housing Act
available, and I understand that under the National Housing Act units are not approved that have no running water and depend on septic tanks and so forth for sewage disposal.
These two solutions, the co-operative housing scheme and the suggestion that we might be satisfied with a more practical form of low-cost housing at the moment, depend very much upon local community action. In fact it seems to me that most of the provisions of the National Housing Act are quite useless unless municipalities, provinces, co-operative building groups and even the local contractors are willing to take advantage of the terms of the legislation and exert some initiative at the local community level toward the solution of these difficulties.
That leads me to suggest that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation might do something by way of propaganda and publicity to try to stimulate local enthusiasm and encourage local groups to participate under the terms of the legislation. I think Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has the necessary public relations machinery to do such a job. Certainly the government has, because as we contemplated the appearance of this legislation quite a feeling of anticipation was built up. It looked as if it were going to be the summum bonum as far as our housing problems were concerned. We were all on our toes hoping to find that at last we had the answer to the riddle; and it could be that the legislation will be helpful if the provinces accept their responsibility, and if something is done about the basic difficulty of inequitable distribution of tax resources, financial resources and service responsibilities.
I saw a newspaper announcement to the effect that C.M.H.C. is opening further regional offices in order to promote the construction of houses under this legislation. Indeed, I think it is even contemplated that the facilities of the regional office in the city of Brandon may be expanded in order to make it easier for local citizens to become fully informed as to the nature of the legislation and be governed accordingly. Certainly if we are going to meet the really urgent need-and this legislation does not provide a solution because, as I have indicated, of the increasing high cost of home construction -it is going to be met not because of the initiation of this legislation by the federal parliament but by action on the local level.
This question also has broader economic significance. We are very reluctant to talk about the process of economic readjustment, as it is politely referred to, that is going on throughout the continent at the present time. No one dares to use the word "depression".

We use the word "recession", and the term the economists are using today is "economic readjustment", a period of transition to a more realistic economic state of affairs, a moving away from the inflationary buoyancy that has carried the two major countries on this continent forward in an intoxicating state of artificial prosperity since world war II. If there is such an adjustment taking place, and public opinion seems to be crystallizing around the idea that there is, we should not ignore the possible impact of a stimulation in the housing construction program because the economy of every community and city throughout the country has benefited as a result of the construction activity that has gone on since the war.
I have prepared a few statistics to point up just what this means in terms of man hours. These are rough averages. If each housing unit constructed involves 2,300 man hours on the site and 3,100 man hours offsite, we have 5,400 man hours of labour per unit. Taking a full working year as 2,000 hours and the average housing production per post-war year as 80,000 units, work is provided for 92,000 men in the construction industry itself and 124,000 in the industries producing and distributing building materials, a total of 216,000 men, a significant figure indeed.
I will not have the opportunity of serving on the committee that will consider the bill, but I trust that the recommendations that have been made during this very interesting debate will be taken into consideration and that something really constructive will be done to provide through this legislation a solution to the problem of the lower-salaried, younger Canadian citizen.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate on housing there are a few observations I wish to make. The first is that in the constituency of Middlesex East, which I have the honour to represent, there are no slums, so the minister can forget all about slum clearance. However, this fact does not relieve the authorities, municipal, provincial or federal, from taking part wherever possible in the introduction of a modern, realistic housing program to provide homes in modern communities for people who need them and are in a position to purchase them.
So far as housing is concerned, however, the truth of the matter is somewhat similar to the truth of the matter as far as markets for primary products are concerned. We have priced them out of the reach of many prospective buyers. When it is necessary to have an income of $3,800 to purchase a home

under Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, that eliminates quite a large number of people, especially young people who are just getting established.
As the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) pointed out, probably no other activity pumps money into the economic bloodstream to the same extent as the construction of buildings, particularly houses. So many different things are needed in the building of a home that money spent for that purpose is scattered throughout the whole country. I have said time and again that the more people we have owning homes in Canada, the better off we as Canadians will be.
It has been mentioned that the banks are going to be guaranteed on these loans; but do not let us forget what happened in the United States not so many years ago when the banks in that country were not able to meet the demands of their depositors, and declared a bank holiday. This was brought about because the liquid assets, so-called, of those banks were tied up in real estate. We can point with pride to the ability of our banks always to be in a position to meet the demands of depositors. I am not certain that this venture into making loans on real estate is a good move so far as our banking system is concerned.
Then I would point out to prospective purchasers of houses built under Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation that they should not get the idea that because this is sponsored by that corporation it will result in dream houses for everyone. People must not permit themselves to expect that everything will be just as they might wish it to be, simply because the government is behind it. They will find out, to their sorrow, that such is not the case. True, inspections are supposed to be carried out; but those inspections are for the protection of the suppliers of capital, not for the protection of purchasers of homes. Many purchasers have found that out, to their sorrow, in years gone by. An owner will find, after moving into his house, that there are many defects; and then when he makes complaints the buck is passed around from one to another and no one seems to be able to put a finger on the real culprit.
This is a pretty serious matter, and it has been brought to my attention on more than one occasion. I have gone to see some of these homes and I have found that the purchaser has been the guy who have been left holding the bag. He is the boy who is given the runaround. I know the situation particularly well in London, Ontario. Purchasers in that area were just laughed at 83276-92
National Housing Act
when some of these defects developed. I suggested to the manager at that point that some of the contractors who had not been supplying homes up to the specifications should be dropped. However, apparently they were friends of the government, because my suggestion did not appear to be feasible when I broached the subject to him.
I hope the minister will look into the situation in London. I have in mind the Hale-Trafalgar area in the east end of that city. It is a whole new area. Services were laid, levels were established, and the city did its part. But when the homes were built and the city laid the sidewalks according to the levels supplied from their engineering department, it was found that some of the homes were from 7 to 23i inches below the level of the sidewalks. After one good rain last summer the water backed up in one of those lots until it was within half an inch of the cellar window.
When I brought this matter to the attention of the manager he just laughed about it, but it is no laughing matter so far as these purchasers are concerned. The property to which I have referred depreciated to the extent of a couple of thousand dollars, I would say, because of the condition I have described. Yet the purchaser was in no position to do anything about it. The contractor would do nothing, and neither would Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. The purchaser was just left holding the bag. I know of another case where the lawn, the sidewalk and the whole driveway were under water, and this after just an ordinary summer rain. What will happen if there is a real downpour or a thaw following freezing is fairly clear; they will have water in their basements.
All this has happened in an area that is high and dry, an area with good drainage. There is no reason in the world why the building could not have been done in a proper manner. I took these problems up with the manager of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, but I was just given the royal runaround. One of these properties is at 63 Cornish street, and the other at 32 Stevenson street. If the minister does not believe what I have said he can go down there and look at it himself.
I think the people generally welcome this legislation, but no doubt they are expecting more from it than they are going to get. As the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) pointed out, I am afraid the interest rate is so high that it will discourage some of the young people from participating in the scheme.
