Mr. Speaker, I find myself in the same position as the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale), who spoke earlier this evening. I, too, have been vitally interested in this matter over a period of many years. I was therefore happy when I heard the government was going to introduce a new measure on housing. I was immensely pleased when, upon receiving the bill, I read that according to the title it is for the purpose of the construction of new houses, the repair and modernization of existing houses and the improvement of housing and living conditions.
After reading the title of the bill, 1 read the bill. I was bitterly disappointed. I had expected that this would be one of the major pieces of legislation at this session of parliament, that it would introduce principles that would mean a real upsurge in house construction in Canada. I anticipated that it would introduce new principles that would meet what I think are the three basic requisites at the present time. This is not something that can be postponed for months or years; it is something which must be tackled right now.
The first of these principles would be amendments to the act, or new principles, that would result in a greater impetus in home construction, presented in a way such as to be financially acceptable to those in average and lower income groups. The second would be an effort to see that those who are not in a position now, and perhaps for some time to come will not be in a position, to start owning their own homes, would be enabled to rent homes at low rentals. The third is something which in our estimation is of the utmost importance, and that is through an upsurge of house construction to be able to meet at least in part what is undoubtedly an urgent and severe unemployment situation.
I do not believe, Mr. Speaker, that it is possible to contradict the statement that one type of construction that can do more than any other to activate employment dominionwide from the Atlantic to the Pacific is house construction. House construction entails the supplying of lumber, cement, sand, everything required in the kitchen, plumbing, heating and the electrical fixtures. If you analyse the requirements of house construction you will find that it affects industry, as I said, over the length and breadth of Canada, and in addition it supplies direct employment to all the services employed in construction.
Although that is a phase of employment, it is tied in with Bill No. 102, because it was my hope that there would be such sections

and plans in this government bill as would take care of the unemployment situation. I am greatly disappointed that in my estimation it does not do that, and I can understand why. Today it has been made very definitely clear to hon. members and to the people of Canada that the government does not recognize the seriousness and the urgency of the unemployment situation.

Mr. Speaker, as you know I always bow to the will of the Speaker, and I hope of course that my remarks have been noted and that changes will be brought into this housing bill in principle that will help the unemployment situation.
It was my sincere hope that in this bill the government of Canada would have recognized housing needs to the extent which it is apparent, or at least should I say anticipated, that the President of the United States views the matter of housing. I am going to refer

to that, Mr. Speaker, because of the recognition there and because it brings in a principle which should be included in Bill No. 102, namely the method of providing housing by low rental and by subsidy. With your permission, sir, I should like to quote from the New York Times of this morning at page C-31:
President to ask 1 million houses.
Thirty-five thousand would be subsidized-message today to stress aid for lower incomes.
Washington, January 24. President Eisenhower will ask congress tomorrow to liberalize . . .
Will you note that, Mr. Speaker, and through you the government? I continue:
. . . the government's housing programs to help Americans buy at least 1 million new homes a year.
He will place special emphasis on helping middle and low-income families obtain better housing. Among the proposals will be an experimental program to let low-income families buy inexpensive houses with almost no down payment.
Further on it says:
Another will be the experimental program to "finance inexpensive homes for lower income families". President Eisenhower was expected to ask for at least $5 million for this.
The program, as outlined by the special advisory committee, would allow low-income families to buy homes costing up to $8,000 on 40-year mortgages with down payments as low as $200. It would also allow families to rent such homes with an option to buy them later if they wished.
It is my hope even yet that the minister who introduced and is directing Bill No. 102 will reconsider the principles of housing in Canada, and perhaps himself recommend to the house an expansion of the bill so as to directly or indirectly-we can discuss that in committee-subsidize low-cost housing and low-rental housing in Canada. It is in my estimation a move that is imperative at the present time if we are to meet the urgency of the housing situation.
I read the bill very carefully and tried as well as I could to understand the principles of the bill on second reading. There are without any question of doubt certain minor improvements in the bill and in its operation, but not fundamentally any basic principles as a brand new act, that is, to meet the housing problem. I fail utterly to see why the government ever brought the bill in at all.
It is only my own opinion, but to me it seems evident that one reason the government has seen fit to introduce the bill in its present form is because of a lessening of mortgage money available from the lending institutions under the previous act. The original source of money is tightening and as a last ditch effort, having some idea of the problem, the present bill is brought in with the hope that the banks of Canada will come through with 83276-921
National Housing Act
some mortgage money under this new bill and the necessary amendments to the Bank Act and I presume also to the Bank of Canada Act.
If that is the intent-and I say "if" because I cannot impute motives to the minister-
I am inclined to think that the money will not be available unless the interest rate is such that the average citizen, in particular the low-income citizen, who requires a loan will not possibly be able to pay it.
At the present time under the Bank Act the banks of Canada cannot make mortgage loans from their own bank funds, but I think under the trustee act they can lend trust moneys on mortgages. I know of at least one national bank that has been and is now lending millions of dollars on mortgages at 6 per cent. I cannot conceive of a bank which in the past and at the present has been and is lending trust funds on mortgages at 6 per cent accepting an interest rate, even though established by an order in council, that is less than that for loans of depositors' money. I just cannot conceive of that situation.
If we consider what the banks are getting now for lending trust funds, that is 6 per cent, it seems extremely doubtful that the government will be able to get them to advance their depositors' funds at 5J, 5J or 5f per cent. The government can lay down that rate by order in council but it is in the hands of the banks as to whether they lend the money.
This brings me to what I consider to be a very important phase, that is the matter of interest. I remember an hon. member on the government side saying last week that no hon. member on this side of the house had ever commended the government for anything. He should have checked his Hansard before he made that statement, because I remember distinctly that when I spoke in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne I commended the government and the minister who is introducing this bill on the attitude they had taken under the old act with regard to the interest rate if the money was being lent on mortgage to companies established on a nonprofit basis to build houses for senior citizens or for others in the same category.
I want to thank the government again because some hon. members forget that if we had not had that kind of help-and I speak for the organization with which I am connected in British Columbia-we would not have been able to construct the number of homes we have for senior citizens and others in the same income group.

National Housing Act
Housing is of such importance, and I am certain the minister agrees, that it is not strictly a local or provincial problem. If my information is correct, several provinces of Canada are making direct contributions as grants in aid to non-profit organizations set up under the laws of Canada as companies to construct homes on a self-supporting basis for senior citizens and others in the same category.
Over a period of years British Columbia has contributed in the neighbourhood of one-third of the capital cost. I am subject to correction, but I believe in Saskatchewan it is 20 per cent. I believe in the case of Toronto, in Ontario, they are asking for 5 per cent and I anticipate it will be raised. That is what some of the provinces are doing. Housing is not solely the responsibility of a municipality, a province or a group interested in
trying to do something about it; it is a matter of major concern to the federal government.
I was hoping and I still hope that something can be put in this bill to indicate the acceptance at least in principle of direct financial responsibility by the government in the building of the type of homes I have been discussing.
On motion of Mr. Winch the debate was adjourned.
